---

## How to use this plan

Steps are ordered by dependency. Later steps assume earlier ones exist.
Do not jump ahead.

Each step lists:
- **Files** to create
- **TDD reference** for the specification
- **Done when** — the verifiable completion criterion

Mark a step complete only when its "done when" criterion passes.

Versions for every dependency come from `TDD_01 §2.4` and nowhere else. Before installing
a package, resolve it with Context7; if the pinned version does not exist or is
incompatible, fix the table first and say why in the commit.

---

## CI rollout and the `main` ruleset

CI is not written at the end. It starts in Step 0.1 and each step adds the job (or the check)
that the step makes possible, so GitHub verifies every step as it lands. A GitHub ruleset on
`main` grows in lockstep: **a status check is added as required only after its job has run
once on GitHub** (GitHub lists a check only after it has reported), and never before, or
every PR would be blocked.

Ruleset on `main` (created in Step 0.1): pull request required with **0 approvals** (a sole
owner cannot approve their own PR, `MVP_TRIM_CHECKLIST.md` §7, D7), force pushes and deletion
blocked, conversations resolved. Job names are the ones of `TDD_03 §4`. ("Branch up to date" was part of it
until 2026-11-08: see the note of Step 7.1.)

> **The ruleset exists (owner, 2026-10-31).** The repository became public, so rulesets work on the free
> plan. `main` has the active ruleset (id 26241021): pull request required, squash only, no bypass, and eight required checks (`lint-and-types`, `unit-tests`, `integration-tests`,
> `security-tests`, `e2e-tests`, `security-scan` for api, web and worker). `lighthouse` and `changes` are not
> required. A job joins the ruleset only after it has run once. A task below that calls its job advisory
> because there is no ruleset was written before this date.

| Step | CI work | Add to the ruleset as required |
|---|---|---|
| 0.1 | `ci.yml` with `lint-and-types` (Nx affected lint and type-check, and `format:check`); create the ruleset | `lint-and-types` |
| 0.4 | `integration-tests` job born with Postgres and Redis services: `prisma migrate deploy` on an empty database and `check-rollbacks` | `integration-tests` |
| 0.5 | Dockerfiles for `api` and `worker`; `security-scan` job born: build both images, Trivy (CRITICAL/HIGH fails; unfixed ignored); `nx affected --target=build` joins `lint-and-types` | `security-scan` |
| 0.6 | add gitleaks to `security-scan`; add commitlint, `validate:translations` and `validate:deprecations` to `lint-and-types` | none new |
| 1.1 | `unit-tests` job with Nx affected and coverage thresholds (only for paths that exist so far) | `unit-tests` |
| 1.3 | `integration-tests` now runs the integration suites; `security-tests` job born with the tenant isolation suite | `security-tests` (no bypass) |
| 2.5 | `integration-tests` also runs `pnpm test:contracts` | none new |
| 3.1 | Dockerfile for `web` added to `security-scan`; `e2e-tests` job born with Postgres, Redis, SeaweedFS and Mailpit (magic-link login); `lighthouse` job (PRs only; created in Step 3.2, PR B3c) | `e2e-tests` (`lighthouse` stays optional, as in `TDD_14 §8`) |
| 5.3 | `pooler-tests` job born (PR C): the compose stack with PgBouncer in transaction mode, `pnpm test:pooler` and the `core-database` integration suites through it | none new until the owner decides: **pending owner**, add `pooler-tests` to the required checks of `main` after it has run once on GitHub |
| 5.6 | `validate:plugin-api` (every route maps to a plugin scope or a reason; the routes still to expose only shrink) runs inside `lint-and-types-checks`, born in the PR `feat/plugin-api-coverage-map` | none new |
| 7.5 | Railway deployment config; nothing new in the ruleset | none new |

From Step 0.1 on, a step is not done until **its PR is green on GitHub** with every job that
exists at that point. Thresholds, services and secrets (for example `SNYK_TOKEN`) are added
to a job when that job is created.

### Local gates and CI performance

**What runs where.** Local gates are a convenience that catches problems in seconds; CI is the authority
and cannot be skipped (`--no-verify` is forbidden by `CLAUDE.md`, and the ruleset blocks the merge anyway).
Nothing heavy runs at commit time, so committing often stays cheap.

| Moment | What runs | Budget |
|---|---|---|
| Editor | ESLint and Prettier on save (optional, not enforced) | instant |
| `pre-commit` | `lint-staged` (ESLint `--fix` with `--max-warnings=0`, Prettier, `prisma format`) which fixes and re-stages instead of rejecting; `gitleaks` on the staged files; the translations and rollbacks validators only when such files are staged | under 10 s |
| `commit-msg` | `commitlint`, showing the exact rule that failed | under 1 s |
| `pre-push` | `pnpm validate:affected`: Nx affected `lint` and `type-check`, `format:check`, `validate:deprecations`, `validate:isolation`, translations and rollbacks; no Docker needed; skipped when only `docs/` changed; the unit tests are left to CI (required check `unit-tests`, which also enforces the coverage thresholds) and run here only with `pnpm validate:affected --full` (owner, 2026-11-11: the local test run took 30 to 50 min with the machine swapping) | seconds to a few minutes |
| Before opening a PR (manual) | `pnpm validate:ci`: the full local mirror of CI with the compose services up (integration, contracts, security tests) | minutes |
| CI | every job of `TDD_03 §4`, required by the ruleset as they are born | 5 to 15 min |
| After the merge | staging deploy from `main`, production from a version tag with manual approval (Step 7.5) | n/a |

`TDD_14 §2` calls `validate:all` the pre-push check but defines no hook for it and runs the whole
repository; this plan makes the hook real and affected-only (`validate:affected`), and keeps `validate:all`
as the full local run. `gitleaks` is a local binary (`brew install gitleaks`): the hook fails with a message that
says so, and the README lists it as a prerequisite. Husky is disabled in CI (`HUSKY=0`).

**CI performance and cost.** The repository is private, and a free GitHub plan includes a limited number of
CI minutes per month, so speed and cost are the same goal. Rules for `ci.yml` and every later workflow
(versions of the actions are resolved through Context7 when the file is written and kept current by Dependabot,
always pinned to SHAs):

- **One run per branch:** workflow-level `concurrency` (`workflow` plus `ref`) with `cancel-in-progress: true` for
  pull requests, so a new push cancels the superseded run. Never for `main` or tag runs, which must finish.
- **Least privilege and a ceiling:** `permissions: contents: read` by default, widened per job (for example
  `security-events: write` for the Trivy upload), and a `timeout-minutes` on every job.
- **Affected only:** `actions/checkout` with `fetch-depth: 0` and `filter: tree:0`, then `nrwl/nx-set-shas`, then
  `nx affected`. A docs-only change finishes in seconds.
- **Dependency cache:** `actions/setup-node` with `cache: pnpm`, and `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile --prefer-offline`.
- **Nx task cache, locally only:** `lint`, `type-check`, `test`, `build` and `prisma generate` are cacheable in `nx.json`
  (`targetDefaults` with `cache: true` and `namedInputs` where `production` excludes tests and config of tests), so on a
  developer machine a task whose inputs did not change is replayed, not run. **CI does not persist this cache:** Nx 23
  refuses local cache artifacts generated on another machine ("Unrecognized Cache Artifacts"; it is a cache-poisoning
  safeguard), and every runner is a different machine, so restoring `.nx/cache` with `actions/cache` never produces a hit
  (verified on Step 0.1). CI saves time with `nx affected` and the pnpm store cache. A hosted remote cache (Nx Cloud) is
  the supported way to share task results between runs; it is a later option, not an MVP dependency.
- **Docker:** `docker/build-push-action` with the GitHub cache backend (`cache-from` and `cache-to` of `type=gha`,
  one scope per image) in `security-scan`, and the Trivy vulnerability database cached.
- **Browser suite in slices:** `e2e-shards` runs the Playwright suite in six jobs (`e2e-shard (i/N)`, `E2E_SHARD`; N is the `total` of the matrix, six since the PR that wrote this line, after four and five; each step was measured in its PR), each with its own Postgres, Redis, Mailpit, SeaweedFS and ClamAV; `e2e-tests`, the required check, is an aggregator that waits for them (`if: always()`, red unless every slice passed, or were skipped because `changes` says the web app is untouched). Playwright splits by file and by test count, not by duration; the summary of each slice shows its time, and a slice that grows near its 20 minutes is rebalanced from those numbers. Result of the balance work (PR 373): about half of the time of the specs was waiting for the per-address limit of magic links (5 a minute, a security control that stays), so the api that the e2e config starts takes `E2E_MAGIC_LINK_LIMIT=50` (NODE_ENV=test only, refused anywhere else, never set by a workflow), and the specs wait on that limit instead. Job time of the slices went from 495/201/329/146 s (PR 367) to 290/204/314/136 s, 296/205/339/154 s and 242/197/302/159 s in three runs, with the same 185 cases (47+48+72+18): the longest slice went from 495 s to 302-339 s, at best at the 300 s that was hoped for and usually above it. The owner approved going from four to five slices (2026-11-10, with the security suite in two jobs and the Nx cache, to shorten the longest job of the run); the PR that did it measured the longest slice against four slices, and the measurement is in its description. Each slice still pays about 130 s of preparation, so shards stop paying when the specs of one are under about 2 minutes (the rule below); Playwright splits by file, so the way past that is to split the heaviest files (`fullyParallel` per file once the cases of a file are isolated). The name of a skipped slice shows as `e2e-shard (${{ matrix.shard }}/${{ matrix.total }})` when the web app is untouched (cosmetic, not a required check).
- **ClamAV in the background in `integration-tests` and `e2e-shards`:** a service container holds the start of the job until it is healthy (`Initialize containers` 37-38 s against 18-23 s for the jobs that have no scanner), and the signature database takes most of that. The scanner now starts with `docker run` in `.github/actions/clamav-start` right after the checkout and the job waits for it (`clamav-wait`, up to 6 minutes, then the log of the container and a failure) before the first step that scans a file, so the load overlaps with install, migrate and build. Both jobs still use the same image and the same health check, and nothing that they test changed; the other jobs have no scanner because they use none (checked: `security-shards`, `security-scan` and `lighthouse` carry only services their code reads). The wait fails early (container missing, exited or unhealthy) and prints what the start and the container said; the log of the container is printed when a later step fails. The image pull is in the background too. The tag of the image is written in the action, which Dependabot's docker ecosystem does not read: `pnpm validate:ci-shards` now fails when it differs from the tag of `docker-compose.yml` (which Dependabot reads), so a bump of one is a bump of both (PR 7.3-B2); the start retries a failed pull three times and `clamav-wait` stops early when it gave up.
- **`lint-and-types` in two jobs and an aggregator:** `lint-and-types-code` (checkout, install, nx-set-shas, the public variables of the web build, and lint, type-check and build: `nx affected` on pull requests, everything on main, as before) and `lint-and-types-checks` (checkout, install, the production audit, `format:check`, the commit messages and the title of the pull request, and the seven `validate:*`) run side by side; the required check `lint-and-types` is an aggregator (`always()`, green only when both are `success`; failure, cancelled and skipped are red). No step was removed or loosened: the 18 steps of the old job exist in one of the two (the four of setup in both). Measured on `run-many --all`: lint 116 s, type-check 76 s, build 26 s (one run, as separate steps); the old job took 217-266 s on a pull request over everything. `--parallel=4` was tried and gave no gain (lint 217/250 s against 266/225 s, unit tests 158/160 s against 163/112 s, two runs each), so it stays at 3. Known limit: three more installs of about 25 s run in parallel, so runner minutes grow by about a third; the next critical path is the e2e slices.
- **(History, superseded by the entry below) Security suite in six jobs (was five since PR `fix/ci-security-shards-five`, four since PR 375-385, two before; 184 s against 242 s with two, 155-215 s with three; six since PR `ci/security-shards-6`, after shard 4/5 of the run of #588 died with `JavaScript heap out of memory`, 4055 MB of the 4096 MB heap, as shards 1/4 and 2/4 did in PR #542: the heap is filled by the number of spec files in one process):** `security-shards` runs the six jest shards of `tests/` (`SECURITY_SHARD=1/6` to `6/6`, the latency spec is a step of the last shard, chosen by `strategy.job-total`, so a new count cannot drop it; jest cuts the sorted list of files into slices of the same count, and the three heavy specs, team, realtime and conversations-performance at about 28 s each, made the halves uneven; with four the slowest job took 156 s (134, 131, 156 and 127 s); a custom sequencer needs recorded durations that drift, so it is not built; each shard writes its peak memory to the job summary) in parallel, each in its own job with its own Postgres, Redis and SeaweedFS (historical, measured with four shards: job time from about 370 s to about 156 s, peak memory used on the runner 3.5-3.9 GB of the 16 GB, heap of node 4 GB per process; the six-shard figures are read from the `peak memory used on the runner` line of the first runs); `security-tests`, the required check, is an aggregator that is green only when every shard succeeded. Locally `pnpm test:security` still runs all six one after the other.
- **Security suite in eight jobs (PR `fix/ci-security-shard-balance`, 2026-11-19):** shard 1/6 ran out of the 4 GB heap again (4050 MB at 237 s, no failed test) after the specs of the short contexts of C3 and of F6-3f joined it (34 files in a process); eight shards put 25-26 files in each one and `--logHeapUsage` prints the heap after every file. The required check is still `security-tests` (the aggregate of the matrix), so the ruleset needs no change; `rls-enforced-security` (PR #764) moved to eight by #764 after this PR merged. Debt: the shard is cut by file count, not by weight (a sequencer that balances the app specs would flatten it): Step 7.3.
- **Security suite: the shard count in one validator, and the fresh-process specs in their own job (PR 7.3-B2, `ci/shards-stability`, 2026-11-22):** measured on the last six green runs of `main` (`gh run view`): `security-shard (8/8)` took 310-420 s against 175-300 s for the other seven, and the reason was not the number of files: the main step of the shard (jest) varies 120-241 s from run to run in any shard, while the last shard also ran the latency spec (61 s) and the plan specs of row level security (45 s) as steps after it, 106 s that only that leg paid. They now run in `security-isolated-specs`, a job of its own with its own services and database, beside the shards; `security-tests` (the required check, same name) waits for it as well as for the shards and is green only when both are `success`, so the ruleset needs no change (read only). The `if: startsWith(matrix.shard, ... job-total)` conditions are gone, so a change of the shard count cannot leave those specs without a job. The files are not re-split: the spread of the jest step inside one shard (for example 8/8: 241, 189 and 177 s in three runs) is larger than the difference between shards, which is the noise of the runner, so a sequencer made from recorded durations would chase it. **`pnpm validate:ci-shards`** (CI `lint-and-types-checks`, pre-push, `validate:all`) reads `ci.yml` and `tests/project.json` and fails unless: the matrices of `security-shards` and `rls-enforced-security` are exactly `1/N` to `N/N`, once each, with the same `N`; the local loop of `test-security` runs the same list; `security-tests` needs `security-shards` and `security-isolated-specs`; the e2e slices are `1` to `total`; and the ClamAV image of `.github/actions/clamav-start` equals the one of `docker-compose.yml`, which Dependabot does read (so the hand bump of the action is now a failing check, not a note). The count is still written in the matrix and in the loop (deriving one from the other would need a generated matrix, and the validator makes a disagreement impossible to merge). **ClamAV start:** `clamav-start` tries the pull and the start three times (10 s and 20 s of pause) and writes its outcome; the container restarts up to three times on failure; `clamav-wait` fails at once with the log when the start gave up, instead of waiting its six minutes. **Left on purpose, each with its owner (Step 7.3):** (a) lighthouse already asserts the median of `RUNS_PER_PAGE = 3` runs; the TBT of the inbox (239.5 ms against 200 ms in #888) was a median too, on a PR that touched no web code. Five runs would cost about two minutes of the job and no ceiling is raised; it is not changed without a second failure with a green JS budget, and then the number of runs is the first thing to try; (b) the jest step of a shard is cut by file count (the old debt above) and the weight of a spec is still unmeasured: the open items (a) to (c) of the heap task below are unchanged; (c) the `orders` JS budget of the lighthouse job sits at about 0.14 KB under its 300 KB ceiling: a web PR that adds code there fails and must cut first (Step 7.4 owns the ceilings); (d) `security-isolated-specs` repeats the services block (Postgres, Redis, SeaweedFS) of `security-shards`, like every job of `ci.yml`, so a tag bump touches each copy: a shared definition (anchors or a reusable workflow) is the CI debt of Step 7.3 for all jobs, not of this PR; both specs seed their own data, so the empty database changes nothing. (e) **Ruleset (owner, pending):** no check is added for this PR: `security-isolated-specs` is not a required check on its own because the required aggregator `security-tests` waits for it and reads its result; if the owner prefers it listed, add `security-isolated-specs` to the `main` ruleset. (f) `validate:ci-shards` requires that the aggregator reads `needs.security-isolated-specs.result`, not that its condition uses it (a `true` in its place would pass): Step 7.3-B / 7.7 hardens it. (g) `clamav-wait` breaks on `exited` and, with `--restart on-failure:3`, a brief restart could read as a false failure (rare): Step 7.3-B / 7.7.
- **Security suite: the heap of a shard, fixed at its cause (PR `ci/security-shard-heap`, 2026-11-23):** `security-shard (8/8)` and `rls-enforced-security (8/8)` of #934 died with `Reached heap limit` after 31 files, and the same logs show it was not that shard: every shard grows by 60-480 MB per spec file (the app of each file is never given back by jest 30 with `--experimental-vm-modules`) and ends at 3.7-3.8 GB of its 4 GB (shard 1/8 passed at 3790 MB after 32 files), so any new file moved a different shard over the line. The shards run `--maxWorkers=1 --workerIdleMemoryLimit=2000MB` instead of `--runInBand`: jest 30.5 runs in band whenever `workerIdleMemoryLimit` is undefined and `maxWorkers <= 1`, so setting the limit makes ONE child worker (files still one at a time, one database) that jest replaces when the `heapUsed` of the worker (jest-worker `processChild`, garbage not yet collected included, so it recycles a little early, never late) passes 2000 MB after a file. `--shard` still covers every file, the heap (4096) and the count (8) and the names of the checks are not touched, no spec is skipped. `pnpm validate:ci-shards` now fails a `jest.config.cts` call of `test-security` that has `--runInBand`, no `--maxWorkers=1` or no `--workerIdleMemoryLimit=<n>MB` (`jestInvocationProblems`, five cases in `ci-shards.spec.ts`). **Debt, with owner (Step 7.3):** (a) the retention itself (which spec file keeps what, the likely candidate is the Nest app and the Prisma/Redis clients each file opens and `app.close()` does not free) is not found: the recycling hides it, a spec-leak check is still open; close (a) when the holder is found, or after three runs of `main` whose peak heap per file stays under 2500 MB; (b) the 2000 MB limit is a first measurement, tune it from the heap lines of the first runs (each restart costs the start of a process, a few seconds); close (b) after three green runs of `main` with every shard under 15 min and the peak heap per file under 2500 MB; (c) the `rls-plan` and `latency` configs keep `--runInBand` on purpose (one or four files); (d) the same growth can exist wherever jest runs in band over many files: `apps/api` integration (135 spec files, `--runInBand --coverage`), `apps/worker` (10), `libs/core/database`, `redis` and `audit` (2-3 each). They pass today; owner Step 7.3: read their `--logHeapUsage` before adding files to `apps/api`, and give it the same worker (a coverage run in a recycled worker needs its own check) if it passes about 3 GB.
- **HTTP layer, PR A2 (`fix/http-compressed-body-timeouts-429`, 2026-11-24; H-10, BAN-182/H-12, H-11):** (1) a compressed body (gzip, deflate, br, zstd) that is empty or corrupt reaches the filter as the raw error of the decompressor with a 400 and `expose` and no `type`; `bodyParserRefusal` now recognises it (`BodyParserErrorTypes.CORRUPT_ENCODING`) and answers 400 at warn level, public routes included. (2) `HttpServerTimeouts` (`libs/core/domain/api`) sets `requestTimeout` 120 s and `headersTimeout` 30 s on the server of the api and the worker (`applyServerTimeouts`), instead of Node's roughly 5 minutes. (3) the per-address throttler now refuses with a `PlatformException` that carries `retryAfterSeconds` and sets `X-RateLimit-Limit/Remaining/Reset` next to `Retry-After`; the one-click unsubscribe says the seconds left of its window (`PTTL`); the public data request says at most one day; the web shows the wait through `errorDetailOf` (PR B4: the `errorDetails.rateLimit` message, in seconds up to a minute and in minutes after; A2 had its own `rateLimitWaitOf` and was rebased onto it, so the web has one reader of the wait). **Debts, closed by Step 7.7:** (a) the 429 of `plugin-widgets.service` (`hit`), `exports.service`, `finance-chain.service`, `avatar-uploads.service` and `upload-checks` still carry no `retryAfterSeconds` (the first has a 60 s window and wants the same `PTTL` as the unsubscribe; the others are caps of concurrency with no window, which need a decision of what to say); (b) `X-RateLimit-*` are not in `EXPOSED_HEADERS` of `web-cors.middleware.ts`, because the web reads the body; add them when a browser client reads headers; (c) the 429 of the per-user layer (`spend-user-budget`) sets no `X-RateLimit-*`; (d) `keepAliveTimeout` of the server stays at Node's default: it depends on the idle timeout of the balancer in front, which is not in the repository; (f) the data request says at most one day, not the exact time left (it would need the `PTTL` of both counters; chosen so that the answer is the same for the address and the store); (g) `throwThrottlingException` writes headers on an HTTP response and assumes an HTTP context (the guard is applied to no websocket or RPC route today); (h1) no spec renders the `errorDetails.rateLimit` message for exactly one minute (60 s, 'seconds') or for 15 minutes in both languages (the cases of 1, 45, 61 and 120 s are rendered; the boundaries are asserted on the key and values in `error-message.spec.ts`): add the two rendered cases, **Step 7.7**; (h0) the public data request says at most one day, which the web shows as 1440 minutes (`errorDetailOf` has no unit above minutes: adding hours costs bytes in the shared chunk of the orders screen, which sits at its lighthouse budget; **Step 7.7** with the split of the shared chunk); (h) a request that stays past `requestTimeout` (120 s) gets a bare 408 with no body the web can translate, and no route reads a body that slow today; (i) `plugin-events-body-parser.spec.ts` fails with `write EPIPE` on macOS also on a clean `main` (the 1 MiB case, not touched here), CI on Linux is the check; (e) the spec of the integration route of unsubscribe (`tests/api/notification-unsubscribe.spec.ts`) was extended with the header and was not run on the machine of the author (no private database); the CI job runs it.
- **Worker cron schedules in UTC (PR 7.3-B11, `fix/worker-utc-cron`, 2026-11-22):** the schedules of `Schedules` are written and documented in UTC, but `@nestjs/schedule` runs a `@Cron` in the time zone of the process and none of the 28 declares one, so a worker on a machine in another zone fired at the wrong hour (Asia/Dubai, UTC+4: `RECONCILE_FINANCE`, `30 4 * * *`, ran at 00:30 UTC). `apps/worker/src/utc-timezone.ts` sets `process.env.TZ = 'UTC'` and `main.ts` imports it before `./instrument`; the runtime stage of `docker/node-service.Dockerfile` sets `TZ=UTC` (production was already UTC; that Dockerfile builds the api and the worker, so both images now run in UTC; the web has its own). `utc-timezone.spec.ts` runs a real Node process started in Dubai, once without the module (00:30) and once with it (04:30, and a local date equals its UTC date): Jest copies `process.env` per test, so the zone cannot be proved inside the test process. Rejected: `{ timeZone: 'UTC' }` on 28 decorators (noise, and a new scheduler would forget it; `ScheduleModule` has no global option). `cron` 4.4.0 (the version `@nestjs/schedule` pins) is now a devDependency for the spec. Debt: nothing stops a `@Cron` from being added to the api outside the worker (the api entry would need the same first import); the api has none today. Step 7.3 adds a guard when one joins. The spec runs `.ts` in a child Node, which needs Node >= 22.18 or 24 (`.nvmrc` 24.20).
- **Store currency and the books (PR A3, `fix/store-currency-guard`, FIN-700 and FIN-700b, 2026-11-24):** the books are USD only (TDD_18 §2.8), but `PATCH` and `POST` of a store took any ISO 4217 currency, and an order kept the other currency with the same cents (no scale by exponent), so the entries said USD over a yen amount. Now `OrganizationsService` refuses, inside the same transaction as the write, a currency other than `finance_settings.baseCurrency` once the organization has books (409 `ORG_STORE_CURRENCY_NOT_BASE`, en/es text), and `FinanceSetupService` refuses to set the books up over a store in another currency (both take the chart lock of the organization, so they take turns), and the analytics rollup adds `orders.revenue` over the orders in the currency of the store only (the order count still counts every order). Debts: (a) before the books exist a store may still change currency while it holds orders; whether a store with orders locks its currency is decided in **Step 7.3**; (b) orders already saved in another currency stay as they are and the posting of the books does not check `orders.currency` against the base currency: **Step 7.3**, and the VAT report and `customer-orders` also add saved orders without checking their currency: **Step 7.3**; (a2) the rollup filters by the CURRENT currency of the store, so changing it before the books exist drops the older orders from `orders.revenue` of a period that is re-rolled, and `orders.revenue` now carries the count of the orders in that currency, not of every order: **Step 7.3** (lock the currency of a store that holds orders, which closes both); (c) the store form of the web still lists every currency and shows the 409 only after the save: **Step 7.7** (disable the field when the organization has books).
- **CI round of 2026-11-10 (PRs 366, 367, 373, 375, 378), what is left:** the e2e suite went from about 15 min in one job to five slices (longest 284-305 s; six slices then brought the longest to 240 s and 264 s in two runs, cases per slice 32/42/21/29/43/18 = 185, slices 142-264 s), by a raised per-address magic link limit in the suite's api only (PR 373) and the slices (PRs 367, 378); the security suite from one job of 372-398 s to two of 220-268 s (PR 375). The critical path of a run is now the longest e2e slice (about 285-305 s), then the security shards (about 240 s) and `lint-and-types` (230-255 s). Two improvements were studied and left for later (debts, owner 2026-11-10):
- [ ] **Debt, Nx cache between CI runs (paused):** cache `.nx/cache` only in `lint-and-types` and `unit-tests` (never in `security-tests`, the e2e or `test:security`), keyed by the lockfile with restore keys by branch, plus a check that a broken change (lint, types, test) still fails with a warm cache. Paused because a pull request runs only what changed (`nx affected`, the key of Nx is the hash of the inputs), so the cache does not speed up the first run of a PR, which is what holds merges, only `main` (`run-many --all`, an estimated 254 s to 110-150 s) and later pushes of a PR; it also costs a policy exception, because CLAUDE.md asks `--skip-nx-cache` for the gates the author runs. Resume it if `lint-and-types` or the runs of `main` become the bottleneck again (the critical path of a PR is now the longest e2e slice, about 285-305 s).
- [ ] **Debt, split the heaviest e2e files (next improvement):** with five slices the slice that held `thread.spec.ts` (30 cases in one serial describe, 910 lines, with `settings`, `templates` and `team`: 55 cases, specs 2.5-3.1 min) was the longest, because Playwright splits by file; splitting the heaviest files (`thread.spec.ts` first, by theme, its cases already create their own data), or `fullyParallel` per file once the cases of a file are isolated, would let the shards balance. Worth doing only if the slowest slice is still the critical path: with six slices the longest is 240-264 s (the slice of 43 cases that holds `thread.spec.ts`), close to the security shards (about 240 s) and `lint-and-types` (230-255 s), so it is not the only bottleneck any more.
- **Flaky found in that round, fixed in the PR that wrote this note:** `invitations.spec.ts`, "a link that does not exist says so", asked for `getByRole('alert')` and the page has two (the message and the route announcer of Next), so it failed in strict mode now and then and passed on its retry (run 42794154753, attempt 2, slice 3); it now picks the alert by its message (`en.errors.TENANT_INVITATION_INVALID`). The other specs that ask for an alert scope it to a dialog or a card, or filter it by text (swept in the same PR), so none has the same problem.
- **Rule: the test suites grow, the CI is re-measured at the close of every milestone (owner, 2026-11-10).** (1) The e2e and security suites are split by file across shards that the CI assigns by itself (`E2E_SHARD`, `--shard`): a new spec needs no registration. (2) Write specs small and by theme (a spec file of more than about 300 lines or 25 cases is split when it is next touched; `thread.spec.ts` has 910 lines and 30 cases, so it is split the next time it changes), every case creating its own data and never depending on the order or the state of another, so any file can land in any shard. (3) End-to-end specs are for critical flows from door to door; whatever a unit, integration or component test can prove goes there. (4) At the close of each milestone, read the time-per-spec summary of a recent `main` run: if the slowest shard of a suite is above about 5 minutes, or the whole run above about 7, raise the number of shards (the one `total` of the matrix; the `job-total` step guards that the count of slices equals it; it does not detect a duplicated or a missing index with the same number of jobs, which is checked in the diff of the matrix) or split the heavy spec, and note the measure in this plan; a shard costs about 2 to 2.5 minutes of fixed preparation (services, install, build), so more shards stop paying when the specs of a shard are under about 2 minutes. The baseline at the close of 2026-11-10: with five slices the slowest e2e slice was 284-305 s and a run of a PR about 6 minutes (with six slices the slowest was 240-264 s, see the line above; it is already below the 5 minutes of the trigger). (5) The magic link limit raised for the e2e suite (`E2E_MAGIC_LINK_LIMIT`, only with `NODE_ENV=test`) is the only limit relaxed for tests; no other limit, check, retry or scan is loosened to save time, and the names of the required checks (`e2e-tests`, `security-tests`, ...) stay.
- **Rule: QA is layered, not one big pass (owner, 2026-11-10).** (1) Every step: only the definition of done (unit and integration tests, tenant isolation, `/code-review` by lens, CI gates); no human QA round per step. (2) Risk checkpoints inside a milestone: a short QA (a few hours, a short matrix with abuse and tenant isolation cases) at the points where money, stock or a message to a real customer is born. The step that opens such a point says in the plan, when it starts, "QA checkpoint: yes/no and which cases"; a step that touches none of that says no. For Milestone 4 the checkpoints are: after 4.1-4.4 (orders: money, stock, order lifecycle), after 4.8-4.10 and 4.14 (shipping, labels, customer messages, carrier adapters) and after 4.12-4.13 (returns and COD remittances: money and inventory movement). (3) Close of every milestone: a full QA with two passes (the first with everything, the second short to verify the fixes), as done for Step 7.9. (4) Before the first release: a final QA with the owner's real tests (Meta, carriers). QA reports findings with evidence and severity and does not fix; every P0-P2 becomes one fix PR. Interface-only work (visual polish) is tested at the close of the milestone.
- **Playwright:** the browsers directory cached by Playwright version in `e2e-shards`; system dependencies installed on every run.
- **Jobs in parallel:** no `needs` chain between the test jobs, so the wall time is the slowest job, and each job
  that is not needed for a change is skipped with a **job-level `if`** (a `changes` job decides). A job skipped by
  `if` reports success to a required check; a workflow-level `paths` filter would leave the check pending and
  block the merge, so it is never used.
- **Full run as a safety net:** pull requests run affected only; pushes to `main` and a nightly `schedule` run the
  suites in full, to catch anything the project graph missed.
- **Coverage upload** runs on pull requests (for the diff) and on `main`; the heavy jobs (`e2e-tests`, `lighthouse`,
  image scans) run only when the changed projects can affect them (`lighthouse` on pull requests only).

## Milestone 1 — Auth and tenancy

The security foundation. Everything after this depends on it being correct.

### Step 1.0 — Queues, workers and email
Placed first in this milestone because Step 1.1 sends magic links through the email queue.
- [x] `libs/core/queues/queues.module.ts` — `@nestjs/bullmq`, seven queues plus DLQ (the `ai` queue is DEFERRED)
- [x] `apps/worker`: `LeaderLockService`; the bootstrap, the health routes and the graceful shutdown exist since Step 0.5. Readiness gains the Redis check (`RedisHealthIndicator`, `PING`, with the `ioredis` client of the cache and the queues) in the api and the worker, and in the worker also that at least one BullMQ worker is running (`TDD_04 §4`)
- [x] Email worker + `ResendProvider` (+ Mailpit dev provider) + React Email template mechanism + server-side i18n. The mechanism ships with the `MAGIC_LINK` template, because it needs one to be tested; Step 1.1 only sends it
- [x] Resend webhook with transactional idempotency. A bounce or complaint is logged (address hashed) and counted, not stored: the suppression list that replaces `markEmailInvalid` is a later step (`MVP_TRIM_CHECKLIST.md` → "Email build details (Step 1.0)")

**TDD:** `TDD_07 §1`, `§4`, `§5`
**Done when:** a `SEND_EMAIL` job enqueued from a test is delivered and visible in Mailpit, and
killing the worker mid-job lets the job complete or retry without loss.

### Step 1.1 — Authentication
- [x] `apps/api/src/modules/auth/` — service, controller, JWT strategy. **MVP trim — magic link only:** no password, no Google/OAuth strategy (both DEFERRED)
- [x] Access token 15 min; refresh token 7 days, hashed, family-tracked, rotated with reuse detection
- [x] Magic link login via `VerificationToken` (single-use, short expiry, hashed at rest): request link and consume link (requesting again is the resend; there is no separate resend route). Consuming is a `POST` with the token in the body, never a `GET` with the token in the URL. It issues the access/refresh pair and marks the email verified. Requesting a link for an unknown email returns the same response as for a known one (no user enumeration). Expiry and throttle values per `MVP_TRIM_CHECKLIST.md` §7, D1, D2, held in constants
- [x] Rate limits per `TDD_05 §3.1` (Redis storage), applied to magic-link request and magic-link consume (`MVP_TRIM_CHECKLIST.md` §7, D2; the invitation accept is limited when its endpoint exists, Step 1.4) instead of the login, signup, forgot-password and resend endpoints named there
- [x] `ApiRoutes.auth` and `AuditActions` carry the magic-link request/consume routes and events; the password login, `forgotPassword`, reset and `PASSWORD_*` entries from `TDD_02`/`TDD_05` are not created
- [x] `MAGIC_LINK` email template, sent through the `SEND_EMAIL` job of Step 1.0
- [x] Bull Board at `/admin/queues`, mounted only when `BULL_BOARD_ENABLED=true`; access requires a valid JWT whose `email` claim is in `BULL_BOARD_ADMIN_EMAILS` (empty allowlist = nobody). Applied as middleware, not through `@RequirePermissions()` or `TenantGuard`, because it is cross-tenant. It lives here because it needs this step's JWT strategy. Replay of a dead-lettered job = retry the **failed job in its original queue** from Bull Board (kept by `removeOnFail`); the dead-letter queue is a triage index (see `MVP_TRIM_CHECKLIST.md` §3)
- [x] **MVP trim — closed signup:** there is no public signup endpoint and no Organization, Subscription or `AiCreditBalance` created here. Users come from the seed (Step 0.4) or from invitation acceptance (Step 1.4, which needs the `Invitation` model). The session issuing code (access/refresh pair) is a reusable service so Step 1.4 can call it
- [x] CI: create the `unit-tests` job (Nx affected, coverage thresholds from `TDD_13 §9` only for paths that exist so far). Adding `unit-tests` as a required check is not possible: the repository has no ruleset by the owner's decision (free plan), so the job is advisory

**TDD:** `TDD_01 §7`, `TDD_05 §3`, `TDD_07 §3`, `§5.3`
**Follow-ups found while building** (cleanup of sessions and tokens, `lower(email)` index, timing of the magic-link request, rate limit per store): `MVP_TRIM_CHECKLIST.md` §10. The decisions of this step that differ from the TDD: §3, "Auth build details (Step 1.1)". **Timing of the magic-link request: done (QA AUTH-02, 2026-11-07)**: the api counts the limit and queues `REQUEST_MAGIC_LINK` for any address; the worker looks it up. **Rollout:** deploy the worker before the api (an old worker reads every job of the `email` queue as an email). **Left for Step 7.3, on purpose:** the job shares the `email` queue (concurrency 10, 100/s) with invitations and digests, bounded today by 5 requests per minute per IP; give it its own queue (or a priority) before the api is exposed to the Internet at scale; and re-run the HTTP probe (60 requests of each kind, median and p95) against the staging deploy to confirm the gap is gone.
**Refresh grace (owner, 2026-11-07, PR fix/refresh-grace-window):** a consumed refresh token is accepted once more within `REFRESH_REUSE_GRACE_SECONDS` (10 s) while its successor is unused (`TDD_01 §7`), because a reload with `POST /auth/refresh` in flight lost the answer and revoked the login. Known limits, accepted and tracked in Step 7.4 ("Refresh grace follow-ups"): a third simultaneous request with the same token still revokes the login (the web serializes refreshes with a Web Lock, so the browser does not produce it); the grace leaves two live tokens in the family until it ends (the list of sessions shows one); a grace can race with the use of the successor and leave two branches, as a normal grace does.
**Done when:** the seeded owner can request a magic link (visible in Mailpit), consume it,
and refresh; a magic link cannot be used twice or after expiry; a link requested for an
unknown email returns the same response as for a known one; and refresh token reuse revokes
the session family; `/admin/queues` returns 404 with the flag off, 401 without a token, 403 for an email outside the allowlist and 200 for one inside it; and `unit-tests` is green on GitHub.

### Step 1.4 — Organizations, stores, memberships
- [x] Organization read/update and stores CRUD (`ApiRoutes.organizations.*`); there is no create-organization endpoint (the bootstrap creates it). `StoreSettings` and `RetentionSettings` are created with each store
- [x] `Invitation` flow with mandatory acceptance; `Membership` created on accept. Invitation token: hashed at rest, single-use, expiring, valid only for the invited email
- [x] `GET /invitations/:token` (public): preview only (store, role, inviter, invited email), no other data
- [x] Accept as `POST`, three cases: (a) **no account:** signup with the email fixed to the invited one, creating the `User` (email verified, since the link reached that inbox), the `Membership` and the session in one transaction; (b) **existing account:** requires a session for the invited email (magic link, then back to the invitation page), then creates the `Membership`; (c) **session for another email:** rejected with a mismatch error. Rate limits per Step 1.1
- [x] Web page `/invitations/[token]` (built in Step 3.1) handling the three cases, plus a "no access" screen for users with no membership (revoked invitation, removed from every store). **Not in this step's PR:** Step 3.1 builds and verifies it (its "Done when" lists it); this step ships the API it calls
- [x] Team management endpoints, custom roles
- [x] **MVP trim:** no `EffectivePlanLimitsService` and no `QuotaGuard(SEATS|STORES)`; seats and stores are unlimited

**TDD:** `TDD_01 §4`, `TDD_07 §5.3` (TDD_11 §1.1 effective plan limits is DEFERRED)
**Done when:** the owner can create a store, invite a member by email (no account yet), and
the invitee gets no access until the explicit accept. Accept with no account creates user,
membership and session atomically (a failure leaves no user behind); a reused, expired or
revoked token is rejected; a token cannot be accepted for a different email; signup without
a valid invitation token is rejected; and an authenticated user with no membership is
never sent to `/onboarding`.

### Step 2.4 — Realtime
Two pull requests (owner, 2026-10-26): (1) domain events, (2) gateway, `RealtimeService` and presence. The browser side of the step (connection manager, `useRealtimeSync`, offline queue) moved to Step 3.1, where the web app gets its auth and `apiClient`: it cannot be built or shown working before that.
- [x] Install `@nestjs/event-emitter` (12.0.1, the line of Nest 12; `TDD_01` said 3.0.1) and the `DomainEvents` service in `libs/core/event-bus`: a service announces with `publish(tx, event, payload)` and the event leaves after the transaction commits (`PrismaService.afterCommit`), never for one that rolls back, and a failing listener cannot fail the request
- [x] Emit the `Events.CUSTOMER_*` of `CustomersService` (created, updated, merged, unmerged, identity linked), which Step 2.2 left out because nothing listened to them yet
- [x] Emit from `MessagesService` `Events.MESSAGE_QUEUED` (new: `Events.MESSAGE_SENT` stays for a message the channel took) for a stored reply and `Events.MESSAGE_NOTE_ADDED` (new, without the text of the note) for a note, and `Events.MESSAGE_MENTION` for each mention, which Step 3.5 turns into `NotificationTypes.CONVERSATION_MENTIONED`; from `ConversationsService` the `Events.CONVERSATION_STATUS_CHANGED`, `CONVERSATION_ASSIGNED` (an unassignment is the same event with `assignedTo: null`) and `CONVERSATION_READ`. `CONVERSATION_CREATED` is emitted by Step 2.6, because its payload carries the first message and a conversation is born with it; the unassignment that removing a member does is not announced yet
- [x] Counts of the inbox filters: not cached (`MVP_TRIM_CHECKLIST.md` item 31). Measured by `conversations-performance.spec.ts` over 10 000 conversations: under the 300 ms limit (about 17 ms by hand in Step 2.3). The realtime client refetches them debounced, so the cache would add an invalidation on every write for a query that costs that little
- [x] Socket.io gateway with the ioredis adapter, typed events, a store room and a user room; a conversation room is joined only for a conversation of that store that the user sees (the same visibility as the REST route), and relays typing
- [x] `RealtimeService` + event listeners + `EVENTS_BRIDGE`. What goes out carries ids and no text, and an event about a conversation reaches only the sockets whose user may see it (a note, only who may read notes)
- [x] Per-socket presence with heartbeat and away detection

**TDD:** `TDD_06 §1`–`§5`
**Done when:** two sockets of one store receive each other's events, a socket of store B receives nothing of store A and cannot join its conversations, and closing one of two sockets keeps the user online.

### Step 2.6 — Inbound pipeline
- [x] (PR 1/4) First, move what the worker needs out of `apps/api/src/modules` into `libs/core/messaging` (an Nx library both apps import; the api keeps its controllers): `ConversationsService`, the identity part of `CustomersService`, `RoutingService`, `MessagingWindowService` and the messages writer. `TDD_10 §4` already puts `InboundMessageService` there, and the worker cannot import from `apps/api`; the isolation suite and the tests that import them move with them
- [x] (PR 2/4, with the `reopenWindowDays` migration: `reopen_window_days` is nullable, `null` by default, and `TDD_01`, `TDD_09 §3.3` and the inbox settings API say so) System lines in the thread: `ConversationsService.applyStatus` writes a `MessageType.SYSTEM` message in the same transaction for each change of status that people care about (resolved, reopened, archived, marked as spam or not, snoozed and woken) and `assign` / `assignIfFree` one for each assignment, authored by `system`, with the event, the people and the dates in `metadata` and no text. They do not count as the last message of the list, do not move `lastMessageAt`, do not raise `unreadCount`, are left out of the exports of the customer's messages, and a bulk action writes one for each conversation. Step 3.2 only draws them
- [x] (PR 3/4) `ChannelWebhookController` (verify, normalize, enqueue) + `InboundProcessor`
- [x] (PR 3/4; the reading of the connection is `ChannelConnectionResolver`, the management comes in PR 4/4) `InboundMessageService`: connection → store resolution, identity, reopen/wake/create, dedupe, media job, routing (`RoutingService.apply(storeId, conversationId, { text, receivedAt })`, for a conversation it creates and for one it reopens that has no assignee or whose assignee left; the channel and the customer are read from the conversation), `CustomerIdentity.lastInboundAt` (it opens the messaging window), events (billing window DEFERRED). A message of the customer continues the conversation that customer already has on that channel (owner, 2026-10-26: one continuous thread per customer and channel, like a chat, with the whole history in it): it wakes a snoozed one and reopens a resolved or an archived one through `ConversationsService.applyStatus` (actor `'system'`, reason `CUSTOMER_REPLIED`), the previous assignee keeping it. `StoreSettings.reopenWindowDays` changes with it: it becomes optional, `null` (the default) meaning a new conversation is never started and a number meaning one is started after that many quiet days; the migration with its rollback, the inbox settings API and the text of `TDD_09 §3.3` change in the first PR of this step, and a spam one stays spam (stored, no reopening); it moves `lastMessageAt` and raises `unreadCount` and `lastInboundAt`, and does not touch `lastOutboundAt` or `firstResponseAt` (those are the agent's, set by `recordReply`)
- [x] (PR 5/5) Outbound: the queue and job constants in `libs/core`, and a processor that takes a `queued` reply of `MessagesService`, calls the plugin's `sendMessage` and writes `sent` or `failed` (`deliveryError` holds an `ErrorCode`), with the provider's `delivered`/`read` status callbacks written by the inbound path; the channel limits of the text (WhatsApp 4096, Messenger 2000, Instagram 1000) are checked here, because `POST /messages` only caps at 4096
- [x] (PR 4/5; the outbound processor is PR 5/5) `ChannelConnection` management + `libs/core/crypto` encryption + health scheduler
- [x] **MVP trim:** no `UsageMeteringService`; inbound conversations are never metered or blocked (checked 2026-11-07: `UsageMeteringService` exists nowhere in `apps` or `libs`)

conversation and message in store B only, a replayed webhook creates nothing, and the
endpoint answers in under 300ms p99 while the worker does the work.

- [x] **Web widget, server side (owner, 2026-10-29; PR 2a):** `libs/channels/web-widget` (`WebWidgetPlugin`, declares `TEXT` only and has no messaging window; `connect({ siteOrigins })` makes a site key `pk_widget_…` that is the `connectionId`, keeps the normalized origins in `metadata.allowedOrigins` and no credentials). The visitor token is an HMAC-SHA256 over `{siteKey, visitorId, exp}` (1 hour) whose key is derived from `JWT_SECRET` with a purpose label, so no new variable exists. The token is to the widget what the signature is to a provider: `validateWebhookSignature` reads it from the header `x-widget-token`, and `handleWebhook` reads `{visitorToken, clientMessageId, content}` and emits `message_received` with `externalId` `<visitorId>:<clientMessageId>`, so that sending twice stores once and two visitors cannot collide. Api module `widget`: `POST /widget/bootstrap` (token, store name, `away` from the business hours, the last 50 messages of that visitor: text that reached them, not notes, system lines, queued or failed replies, nor deleted messages), `POST /widget/messages` (queued through the new `InboundEventQueue`, shared with the provider webhook, so the worker stores, routes and announces it like any other), per-request CORS against `allowedOrigins` (the preflight, which carries no key, is answered for the origin that asks and grants nothing; the request that follows checks the list and only then lets the browser read the answer), limits of 30 and 60 a minute per address, and the `/widget` socket namespace (token in `auth`, a listed origin, 5 sockets per visitor, closed when the token expires) with `WidgetDeliveryListener`, which pushes a reply the channel took (`MESSAGE_SENT`) to the room of its visitor as `widget.message` (id, `from` visitor or team, text, date; nothing about agents). Cases in `tests/api/widget.spec.ts`, and "a widget site key" in `tenant-isolation.spec.ts` (a key from the site of another store, and a visitor id that exists in two stores). **Left for later:** files from the visitor and `POST /widget/upload-url` (Step 3.4), typing and read receipts (the typing task of Step 3.2: `TYPING_INDICATOR`, `CUSTOMER_TYPING` and `READ_RECEIPTS` are declared only then), the pre-chat form and linking by email (Step 3.3), and the bundle (PR 2b). **Known limits:** the site-key lookup and the history read run with no store context, so Step 7.1 turns them into the `SECURITY DEFINER` function it already lists; the connection is read from the database on every call (cache it if it shows in the P99); a visitor past 5 tabs is refused, not rotated, and the count is looked at in the handshake, so a burst of connects at once can pass it by a few; a visitor token cannot be revoked, so after a disconnect only the replies stop at once (the listener asks for an active connection), while a removed origin (also by `PUT .../widget/origins`, which refuses new calls at once but does not close the sockets already open) or a copied token lives until the token expires (1 hour); the listener reads one message for every `MESSAGE_SENT` of any channel, which is cheap (one row by id) and can be narrowed with a marker in the bridged payload if outbound volume grows; the generic webhook answers 404 for `web_widget` by id, so a second channel with a door of its own would need a flag on the plugin instead of another `!==`; the token key is derived from `JWT_SECRET`, so rotating it ends every open widget session and the `.env.example` placeholder is accepted outside staging and production exactly as it is for the access tokens

Styles are a constructable stylesheet in a shadow root, so no `<style>` or style attribute exists; a browser without constructable stylesheets gets no widget. `GET /channels/connections/:id/widget` returns the site key, the origins and the snippet (`WIDGET_SCRIPT_URL` in the env), and `PUT /channels/connections/:id/widget/origins` replaces the origins and keeps the key (the bad entry is named by its position, audited as `channel.widget_origins_changed`); both are drawn by Step 3.6. - [x] Messages written in the provider's own app (owner, 2026-10-28): a new SDK event `message_echo` (customer's `channelIdentity`, the message with its `media[]`, `externalId`) that the core stores as a sent message of an external author (`AuthorType.EXTERNAL`, no `authorId`). It is deduplicated against our own sends by `channelMessageId` (the provider echoes those too), and it neither opens the messaging window nor raises the unread count nor is routed. A conversation that is resolved, snoozed or archived is reopened, as a reply of an agent does (owner, 2026-10-28), never spam; a customer with no conversation gets one, unassigned and read, announced as created. It retries while one of our own replies to that customer has no provider id yet, and stores it as the owner's on the last attempt. This replaces "an echo is dropped and counted" of `TDD_10 §6.7`. **Built in PR 1b:** the core, the SDK and schema, the worker case, and the WhatsApp mapping of `smb_message_echoes` (Meta's reference, read 2026-10-28: `message_echoes[]`, `from` the business, `to` the customer; `revoke` and `edit` are skipped; a reaction becomes an external reaction). That field only exists for a number in Coexistence, which needs Embedded Signup (Phase 2), so it is proved by unit tests until a real number does (a box in Step 7.3). **Built in PR 1c:** Instagram and Messenger map `is_echo` (an echo whose sender is not the account is skipped). **Still open:** the app must be subscribed to the `smb_message_echoes` field (the rest of this line is a box of Step 7.3, "Subscribe the WhatsApp app to `smb_message_echoes`")
- [x] Reactions (moved here from an orphan decision of `MVP_TRIM_CHECKLIST.md`, "WhatsApp plugin build details", item 11, which no step carried): the `message_reactions` table, the SDK event `message_reaction`, `message.reaction` in real time, reactions returned with each message, WhatsApp emitting them instead of dropping them, Instagram (`message_reactions`) and Messenger mapping them, and the `REACTIONS` capability declared by the plugins that map them. **Built in PR 1b:** the table with its rollback (a customer by identity, an agent by user, the owner of the provider's app as one `external` reactor), the event and its schema, `MessageReactionsService`, `message.reaction`, `reactions` in each message of the thread, and WhatsApp emitting them and declaring `REACTIONS`. **Owner, 2026-10-28: an agent reacting is in the MVP too, built in PR 1b-2:** `PUT /messages/:id/reaction` (`AuthGuard` + `TenantGuard` + `MESSAGES_SEND`; body `{ emoji }`, null takes it back), `ChannelPlugin.sendReaction` (required by `REACTIONS`, implemented by WhatsApp), the job `SEND_OUTBOUND_REACTION` on the outbound queue, `MessageReaction.deliveryStatus` / `deliveryError` (queued, sent or failed, with a code of ours; shown in each reaction of the thread so that nobody believes the customer saw what the channel refused), and the `messageReaction` case in `tenant-isolation.spec.ts`, which removes the exemption. The core accepts any message that has a `channelMessageId` and a channel that declares `REACTIONS`; the plugin refuses what its provider does not allow. **Known limits:** a reaction taken back that the channel refuses is logged, not shown (its row is gone); a reaction left `queued` because Redis was down is queued again by the same sweep as the replies (`OutboundRequeueScheduler`, with the version it had) and marked failed after an hour, so it never stays "sending". two jobs of the same reaction that run at the same time (an emoji and the next one, a few milliseconds apart) are not ordered, so the provider can end with the older emoji while the thread shows the newer one as sent; the version guard only stops the older job from settling. **Built in PR 1c:** Instagram and Messenger map the customer's reactions (`reaction{action, emoji, mid}`; `unreact` takes it back) and send an agent's (`sender_action` `react` / `unreact`), both declaring `REACTIONS`. The reaction of the account itself is not read: it comes back as the echo of our own send. **Accepted for the MVP (owner Step 7.3 if one is ever hit):** the "Known limits" above are commitments, not open work.
- [x] **Delete and edit a message (owner, 2026-10-28; PR 1d, after 1c):** the core stays channel-agnostic and the plugin decides what its API allows. (1) **Delete is for everyone only:** there is no "delete for me", because in a team inbox it would show the agent a thread the customer does not have (a junk or abusive inbound message is handled with the `spam` or `archived` status of the conversation, a wrong reply with a correction message). Capability `DELETE_MESSAGE`, optional `ChannelPlugin.deleteMessage`, the same queued, sent or failed state as a reaction, shown in the thread; a channel without the capability answers 409 and the inbox hides the action. The permission `MESSAGES_DELETE` exists and has no handler on purpose until now. (2) **Edit reaches the customer or does not happen:** capability `EDIT_MESSAGE`, optional `editMessage`; without it the core answers 409, never an edit that only the inbox shows, and the inbox offers "send a correction" (a new message). Revisions are kept (`MessageRevision`, tenant-scoped, with its isolation case and rollback). (3) **Internal notes** are working data shared by the team, so anyone who can see notes (`CONVERSATIONS_VIEW` and `MESSAGES_INTERNAL_NOTE`) can edit one; the author stays the author, every edit keeps a revision (who, when, the text before) and the note shows "edited by"; an edit carries the version it saw and a stale one answers 409 `RESOURCE_CONFLICT` with the current text, so nobody overwrites a change they did not see. Deleting a note is for its author or `MESSAGES_DELETE`. Edits and deletes are pushed in real time (`message.edited`, `message.deleted`, as `message.reaction` is), so a teammate sees the change without reloading. (4) **Inbound:** SDK events `message_deleted` and `message_edited` for the customer and for the provider's own app (the echo of WhatsApp that carries `revoke` and `edit` is skipped today), applied by the core whatever the author. (5) **A message the customer deleted** shows "the customer deleted this message" to the team; the original text is kept for a short time (store preference, 30 days by default) for disputes, shown only with an explicit permission and every view audited, then a job purges it. (6) **Permissions (owner, 2026-10-28):** no `MESSAGES_EDIT`. A user with `MESSAGES_SEND` edits and deletes their own message to the customer (when the channel can); `MESSAGES_DELETE` (only `admin` has it) deletes the message of another team member; nobody edits the message of another person, a correction is a new message; nobody deletes a message of the customer, it becomes the tombstone of (5). Every delete is audited with who and when **Built in PR 1d (2026-10-29):** the capabilities `DELETE_MESSAGE` and `EDIT_MESSAGE` and the optional hooks `deleteMessage` / `editMessage` (the registry requires the hook of a declared capability); no official plugin declares them, because Meta offers no API to delete or edit a sent message (WhatsApp Cloud API, Messenger and Instagram: nothing in Meta's list of webhook events or send endpoints, read 2026-10-29), so the outbound path is proved with the contract plugin of the suite and a plugin that can (a remote one) needs no change in the core. `PATCH /messages/:id` and `DELETE /messages/:id`, `GET /messages/:id/deleted-content`; `MessageRevision` (migration with its rollback, which also gives the new permission to the Admin roles that exist); `Message.version`, `editedAt/By`, `pendingContent` + `editStatus`, `deletedAt/By`, `deleteStatus`, `changeRequestedAt`, `contentPurgedAt`; jobs `SEND_OUTBOUND_EDIT` and `SEND_OUTBOUND_DELETE` on the outbound queue (a sweep queues again after 2 minutes and fails after an hour, as for reactions); `message.edited` and `message.deleted` in real time (a note only to who may read notes); permission `MESSAGES_VIEW_DELETED` (Admin only) for the kept text of a deleted message, every read audited (`message.deleted_content_viewed`) and every delete audited (`message.deleted`); the purge is an hourly cron (`PURGE_DELETED_MESSAGES`) with `DeletedMessageRetention.DAYS` = 30, which also clears the text of the revisions; inbound SDK events `message_edited` and `message_deleted` applied by `InboundMessageChangesService` whatever the author (the lookup of the target message is shared with reactions in `InboundMessageTargets`); Messenger maps `message_edits` and the `is_deleted` flag of `messages` (both directions: the customer's, and the owner's own echo). **Decisions made while building:** (a) an edit of a reply the customer has changes nothing in the thread until the channel takes it (`pendingContent`, `pendingEdit` in the view), and one the channel refuses leaves the text as it was; (b) a deletion the channel has not taken leaves the message shown with `deleteStatus` queued; (c) the retention is a constant, not a store preference (Phase 2, as the profile staleness); (d) `deletedContent` answers 404 for a message that was not deleted or whose text is purged, and for a note to who may not read notes; (e) an agent's deletion of their own reply needs `MESSAGES_SEND`, the deletion of another person's `MESSAGES_DELETE`. **Bulk deletion measured (2026-10-29):** a customer who deletes many messages at once is one `message_deleted` event and one job for each message; 100 messages of one customer with 20 jobs at a time take about 0.5 s in `tests/api/inbound-message-changes.spec.ts` and leave 100 tombstones and 100 `message.deleted` events, so no batching was built; the cap of 100 events per request only splits the queueing in batches, it drops nothing. The client of Step 3.1 must debounce its invalidation of the thread. **Not verified with a real payload:** the `message_edits` shape of Messenger (`message_edit{mid, text, num_edit}`, taken from Meta's reference) and the `is_deleted` of `messages` (a box in Step 7.3); Instagram's `message_edit` event (changelog of 2026-09) carries no text as far as known, so the plugin skips it, and Instagram's unsend arrives through `is_deleted`. **Follow-ups, none blocking:** (1) the search over message text (`search_vector`) is generated from `content`, so a deleted message stays searchable until it is purged: the search of Step 5.1 must filter `deleted_at IS NULL`; (2) the media of a deleted message stays until Step 3.4 decides what the purge does with files; (3) the thread of Step 3.2 draws the tombstone, "edited", the pending state and the failed one, and the `version` it sends back when editing a note; (4) `editedById` and `deletedById` have no foreign key to `users`, like an audit trail: the user may be removed and the name goes with the member list; (5) editing a note keeps its `mentions` as they were (no one is notified again, and a removed mention stays): decide with the thread of Step 3.2 whether an edit recomputes them; (6) one request at a time for a message: asking to delete a reply whose edit waits answers 409 (and the other way round), so each settles on its own; (7) the purge takes the oldest due rows first across all stores, which is fair enough for one owner and becomes a per-store batch in Phase 2
- [x] **Discard a reply that failed for good (owner, 2026-11-07; PR feat/discard-failed-message):** a reply of the team whose send failed and that the channel is KNOWN not to have taken can be thrown away from the thread. (1) `POST /messages/:id/discard` (204, twice is once), with the permission to send it again (`MESSAGES_SEND`, or `MESSAGES_SEND_TEMPLATE` for a template). (2) Only a message of the team (not a note or a customer's) with `deliveryStatus` failed, no `channelMessageId` and `failureDefinitive = true`. The worker sets `failureDefinitive` when it settles a failure: true for a refusal of the provider (even one retried to the end, a throttle) and for a check that failed before anything was sent; false for a timeout or a network error, a plugin that says `outcomeUnknown`, an answer that made no sense, a failure reported by a receipt, and any failure where an earlier attempt had an unknown outcome; null for a failure from before this existed (such a reply cannot be thrown away, only sent again). A reply that may have gone answers 409 `MESSAGE_DISCARD_OUTCOME_UNKNOWN`. (3) Nothing is said to the channel and no note is added to the thread. The row gets `discardedAt` and, like any deleted one, `deletedAt`, `deletedByType` agent and `deletedById`; every read of the thread leaves it out (the thread, the quote of a reply, the target of a reply, the preview of the conversation, the export; the widget already left out the deleted). (4) The text is kept with the retention of the deleted ones (`DeletedMessageRetention`, 30 days, read with `MESSAGES_VIEW_DELETED`): it is the agent's own words, nothing of a customer, and it lets a supervisor recover what was written if a reply was thrown away by mistake. (5) The files of the reply are removed (their rows); the hourly sweep of stray files takes the objects from the bucket within a day. (6) The audit has `message.discarded` (who, when, the kind of message and the code of the failure, never the text) once per discard. (7) Realtime: the event `message.deleted` of the deletion that already exists; the clients read the thread again and the reply is not in it. (8) Resending a failed reply keeps the doubt: a failure that was definitive starts the new attempt clean, one that may have gone (or from before this existed) leaves the message marked, so a later clean refusal does not make it discardable. (9) A failure is definitive only if the plugin AFFIRMS it, never by default: `PluginError.refused` (the provider answered that it did not take the request: set by the Meta plugins for a throttle, a rejected token, a closed window, a template that is not approved and any other answer of the provider that is not an outage) or a code of a local check made before anything was sent (a channel that takes no files, a file too big or of a type it does not take, a connection that is not there, a file that is gone). A plugin that fails without saying so, `CHANNEL_MESSAGE_FAILED` included, leaves a reply that can be sent again and not thrown away. (10) The worker reads the mark when an attempt begins and writes it (false while queued) BEFORE the provider is asked, so a process that dies mid-send or a job that stalls leaves the doubt; a clean refusal with nothing before it that may have gone takes the mark off, and the failure that ends the send is definitive only then.

- [x] **Name and photo of an Instagram or Messenger customer (owner, 2026-10-29; built in PR 1c-2):** the webhooks carry only the scoped id, so the customer shows as a number. Optional `ChannelPlugin.fetchProfile(ctx, channelIdentity)` returning `{ name?, username?, avatarUrl? }`, required by a new capability `CUSTOMER_PROFILE`. Instagram: `GET graph.instagram.com/<IGSID>?fields=name,username,profile_pic` (name may be null). Messenger: `GET /<PSID>?fields=first_name,last_name,profile_pic`, which needs the "Business Asset User Profile Access" feature requested in the Page settings (an owner step, documented in the connect view). A worker job `FETCH_CUSTOMER_PROFILE` on a queue of its own, `customer-profiles` (5 at a time, 3 attempts, exponential 60 s; a provider that answers slowly fills it and delays no customer message; the heavy queue has no consumer until Step 3.4 and one added now would swallow the `fetch-inbound-media` jobs that wait there, and the inbound queue is where messages wait), one per identity (job id), queued when the identity is created and again when `profileFetchedAt` is older than 7 days (a constant in `libs/core`), always after the message is stored, never inside the webhook and never blocking it. **Stored in new columns of `CustomerIdentity`** (migration with its rollback; the table is already covered by the isolation spec): `username`, `avatarUrl`, `profileFetchedAt`, `profileRetryAfter`, `profileFetchError` (a code of ours). No index: staleness is decided from the identity row an inbound message already reads, and no sweep exists. `displayName` takes the name; a read that finds something replaces name, username and photo link together (the stored link expires), and one that finds nothing keeps what was stored; `Customer.name` is set only while it is null, because the customer's own name is the agents'. A failure retries three times with backoff; when they run out, `profileFetchError` is written, and `profileFetchedAt` too only if the failure was a refusal, so that a refused read is not asked again until the profile is stale; an outage is no answer, so it sets `profileRetryAfter` (one hour ahead) and leaves the date of the last real read alone, and the connection view can tell the owner what is missing. **The photo is a reference only:** no storage exists until Step 3.4 and a plugin never stores anything (the core stores what `fetchMedia` and `fetchProfile` hand over); Meta's urls are signed and expire, so Step 3.4 carries the avatar download through the SSRF-safe fetch. **Built:** `fetchProfile` returns null when Meta has no profile to show (an empty object, or error 2018218 of an account made with a phone number), which is stamped like a read and never retried; `ProfileRequester` (after a stored customer message) and `ProfileFetcher` (the job) in `apps/worker/src/inbound`, `CustomerProfileService` in `libs/core/messaging`, and the `CUSTOMER_PROFILE` capability mapped to Step 3.2 in `scripts/frontend-coverage-map.ts`. Display fallback, drawn in Step 3.2: name, then `@username`, then "Instagram customer ····1234", with an initials avatar
- [x] Follow-ups of the profile fetch found in the review of PR 1c-2, none blocking: (1) the requester repeats the connection and identity lookups that `handleMessageReceived` already did, two indexed queries per Instagram or Messenger message; return the identity from the service and check `needsProfileRead` on it first **(done, checked 2026-11-07: `ProfileRequester` checks `needsProfileRead` on its own identity read before queueing)**; (2) the plugin call is not aborted when the 10 s timeout fires, because `ChannelContext` carries no `AbortSignal`: add one to the SDK and to `MetaGraphClient` **(done in PR `fix/profile-read-abort`: `ChannelPlugin.fetchProfile` takes an optional `signal`, `ProfileFetcher` aborts the signal it hands over when `withTimeout` gives up or the read fails, `MetaGraphClient` joins it to its own limit, and the Meta plugin hands it over; covered by tests of the client, the plugin and `tests/api/customer-profile.spec.ts`; other `ChannelPlugin` methods still take no signal: the SDK has no use for one until a call is slow enough to need it)**; (3) Step 3.4, when it stores the avatar, must fetch it through the SSRF-safe fetch with an https-only, public-host check, and Step 3.2 must draw the stored link with the CSP `img-src` of the app (a link the plugin chose is untrusted) **(checked 2026-11-07, nothing to build: the server never fetches the link, it stores it after `isPlainHttpsUrl`; the web draws it with `RemoteImage` (`referrerPolicy="no-referrer"`, initials when it fails) under `img-src` limited to `*.fbcdn.net`, `*.cdninstagram.com` and `platform-lookaside.fbsbx.com` (`CUSTOMER_AVATAR_IMAGE_HOSTS`, `apps/web/lib/security-headers.ts`); the widget draws no customer photo. If a step ever downloads the photo, it uses the SSRF-safe fetch)**; (4) a username the channel stops giving stays until a read gives another (the photo link is the only field replaced as a whole) **(accepted for the MVP; the box in Step 7.3 "Left by Step 2.7 and 2.8" keeps it)**

The ones seen: `hears an event of the bridge whose ids come in capitals`, `hears an event of the worker, which holds no sockets, through the bridge`, `does not take a user out of a room on the word of an event that the conversation does not bear out`. All three publish to `EVENTS_BRIDGE_CHANNEL` and wait for a socket to hear it. **Hypothesis, not proved:** (1) `EventsBridge.onModuleInit` subscribes inside the `ready` handler and nothing waits for it, so `createTestApp` can return before the api listens; (2) an event is passed on by the one instance that claims it in Redis, so an instance left open by an earlier test of "across instances" can claim it and the socket of the test never hears it. **How to close it:** reproduce in a loop (the spec alone, 20 runs) with a log of which instance claims each event; if (1), make the bridge expose a promise that settles when the subscription is acknowledged (it also fixes the order of a real boot) and have the suite await it; if (2), close every extra instance in a `finally`; if it is neither, say what it was. Do not widen waits or add retries to hide it. **Done when:** `realtime.spec.ts` passes 20 runs in a row alone and the whole integration suite passes three runs in a row. Step 3.1 relies on realtime, so it starts after this. **Closed:** it was both. (1) The bridge subscribed in the `ready` handler and nothing waited for it: `EventsBridge.subscribed` settles when Redis acknowledges, and `createTestApp` awaits it. (2) An api left running on the laptop (`dist/apps/api/main.js`) listened to the same channel and claimed events: `assertNoOtherBridgeListener` stops the suite and names the cause. Proved with 20 runs of the spec alone and three whole integration runs (1057 tests each)

Known limit, accepted: while the indicator is on, the customer sees the message as read even if the agent never opened the conversation (the same effect as the blue ticks the agent would send by opening it); a store that does not want that switches the receipts off and WhatsApp then shows no indicator. The check and the mark of "may have gone" are now one step under the lock of the conversation that the Undo takes (conversation, then message; no network call inside; the retry and the idempotency after the mark are those of before). **Known limit, by design (Step 7.x, sends to customers):** an Undo that arrives after that mark (past the 10 s + 2 s of grace) does not take the message back, because a message already on its way to a customer cannot be withdrawn, and the lock is not held while the provider is asked. A retry after an attempt that may have reached the provider is not judged again and its message is never deleted. **Debt (found in review, not new; Step 7.x):** a delayed job and a sweep duplicate for the same message that run together can both pass the claim (the mark cannot tell a live attempt from a retry); the key is the same for both, and a lease column on the message would make the claim exclusive.
