A range ends at the start of today (UTC), because the daily rollup writes a day when it closes. The widget (first of the sidebar by default) reads `GET /analytics/my-performance` (`conversations:view`, the person of the token): resolved today, open now and the first response of the conversations they answered first today, read live from the conversations with the day of the store's own time zone, because an agent holds no `analytics:view` and the rollups lag by up to an hour. New rolled-up metric `agent.first_response_time` (dimension agent, the author of the first reply of a person that is not a note), so the team table has its time column
- [x] The View analytics action of the Quick actions widget (left by PR B6a of Step 3.2; Find customer in Step 3.3 and Create order in Step 4.4 join the same widget): a link to `AppPaths.store.analytics`, shown with the permission that opens the dashboard **Built in PR B:** the link is shown with `analytics:view` (`ClientPermissions.ANALYTICS_VIEW`)
- [x] Scheduled reports (PDF/CSV/Excel), and `GET /analytics/export` (`analytics.export`) as an export of the exports center **Built in PR C1 (the server):** `GET /analytics/export` (`analytics:view` + `analytics:export`, 202, an `Export` of type `analytics` with its filters checked by `analyticsExportFiltersSchema`, which the worker reads back); `GET/POST /analytics/reports` and `PATCH/DELETE /analytics/reports/:id` (`analytics:manage_reports`, with `analytics:view` and, to make or change one, `analytics:export`: a report sends the figures of the store out by email, so whoever saves one holds the right to take them out; the report runs as the last person who saved it). The file is the day-by-day table of the metrics asked (the whole-store ones, `ReportMetrics`), read from the rollup tables only through `readMetricBuckets`, which the dashboard shares, with a row of totals; CSV (the platform's `csvCell`, so a text that starts with `=`, `+`, `-` or `@` is quoted), Excel (a `.xlsx` written by hand with `fflate`, every text an inline string and no formula) and PDF (written by hand, Helvetica, A4 landscape, header on every page, eight metric columns to a page). `ReportDispatchScheduler` (hourly on one replica, `Schedules.DISPATCH_REPORTS`) queues the reports whose own clock has reached their hour (daily every day, weekly on Mondays, monthly on the 1st; from the hour on, so a missed tick is made up for, and never twice in a local day), one job for each report and local day, which carries that day: the period is the day, week or month that just ended before it, in UTC days like the rollup, however late the job runs; `ScheduledReportRunner` (the `exports` queue) checks that the person still has `analytics:view` and `analytics:export` in an active membership (else it turns the report off), makes the `Export` as that person, and queues one `scheduled-report` email for each address (they do not see each other) with the totals in the body and the file attached; `lastSentAt` and the local day stop a second run, and the email jobs have a deterministic id, so a retry does not send twice. Money is in whole units in the CSV and the Excel file (the rollup keeps cents), labelled USD like the dashboard. No migration: `scheduled_reports` has existed since the first migration. Audit: `report.created`, `.updated`, `.deleted`, `.sent` (how many addresses, never which). **Built in PR C2 (the web):** the dashboard has an **Export** button (`analytics:export`) that opens a dialog with the figures to include (the whole-store metrics of `ReportMetrics`, all ticked), the file type (CSV, Excel, PDF) and the period on the screen (`from` and `to` are its UTC days, the last one out), calls `GET /analytics/export` and ends by pointing to the exports center (the kind "Analytics" is now in its filters, and `analytics:export` opens the center); and a **Scheduled reports** link (`analytics:manage_reports`) to `/s/:storeId/analytics/reports` (`AppPaths.store.analyticsReports`, title `analyticsReports`), a table of the reports (schedule, file type, addresses, last sent, state) with create, edit, pause or resume and delete (a confirmation), whose form takes the name, the figures, how often, the file type, the time zone (this browser's, among the zones it knows), the hour and the addresses (one per line or separated by commas). The form is checked with `createReportSchema` of `libs/core` (the api's own schema), so the page refuses what the server refuses, and an edit sends only the keys that changed. Who holds `analytics:manage_reports` without `analytics:export` sees the list and no buttons that write (the api needs both to save). `ClientPermissions` gained `ANALYTICS_EXPORT` and `ANALYTICS_MANAGE_REPORTS`; the api-client has `analytics-reports-api.ts` and `QueryKeys.analytics.reports`; the words are in `messages/routes/analytics.<locale>.json` (the labels of the figures there repeat the ones of `email.scheduledReport.metrics`, and `report-messages.spec.ts` holds both lists to the catalog). Decisions: (1) the export dialog exports the period of the dashboard and has no date pickers, because the dashboard's four ranges are the periods the owner reads; the rejected alternative was a free range, which is the custom range of (b) of PR B and needs its own validation; (2) the reports are their own page under the analytics route, not a panel of the dashboard, so the table, the form and the confirmation load only for whoever opens them.

- [x] **Search analytics, built in PR C3 (API, worker and the web calls; rule 12 decisions and debts with their owners).** `POST /search/clicks` (`AuthGuard` + `TenantGuard` + any search permission; the kind clicked must be one the member may search, else 403; the store is the header's, a `storeId` in the body is a 400; answer 204, the event is queued and never waited for) queues `search.clicked` as a `TRACK_SEARCH` job: the hash of the text (the same keyed HMAC of the search, so a click groups with its search), what the search was asked of, the kind opened and its place in the list; **never the text and never which result** (analytics rows are tied to no customer). The worker checks it with `searchClickDataSchema` (a search of one kind can only have shown that kind) and refuses a click sent as a plain `TRACK_EVENT`. The palette's as-you-type calls are `passive` (the global route's `passive=true`) and leave no `search.performed`; the results page and the box of the top bar search for real and count. `GET /analytics/search?days=` (`analytics:view`) reads `analytics_events` of the store of the header only (every statement filters by it; the window is a bind parameter): for each kind of search, the searches counted, the ones that found nothing and the clicks, plus the texts of the catalog that found nothing (the only text the events keep, never a text with seven digits or an `@`), grouped by their hash, most asked first, 50 at most. The dashboard draws it as a Searches panel (`SearchPanel`). `AnalyticsEvent` has its isolation case in `tenant-isolation.spec.ts` and its exemption is gone (its first reader is this report). **Decisions:** (1) a click is its own event, not an update of `search.performed` (an event is never changed after it is written); the rejected alternative was a `clicked` field written later. (2) The click carries the text so the api can hash it with the key it holds; the rejected alternative was to give the web the hash, which would hand the key (or an unkeyed hash of a phone number) to the browser. (3) The kind clicked is checked against the member's permissions, not the result against the database: a forged click can only add noise to the member's own store, as a forged search can. (4) One route for the click of every kind, not one for each search route.
- [x] **Left by PR C3 of this step (rule 12):** (a) the clicks of the palette count a click and not the search that led to it (its as-you-type calls are passive, so a palette search that finds nothing and is closed is not counted and its text is not kept in the catalog gaps: accepted, the results page and a click count), so the click-through of the report is clicks over searches counted by the results page; a figure "clicks / searches" is read with that in mind: accepted. (b) The report looks back N days from now (the preset's length), so the Searches panel is hidden for the "last month" range (it cannot show a month that is over) until the report takes a from and a to: Step 7.4 (task "From Steps 5.1 and 5.2"). (c) The Playwright cases of the click and the panel run in CI only. (d) A click sent as the page unloads can be lost (`ApiClient` has no `keepalive`), and a middle-click is counted through `onAuxClick`: Step 7.4. A click is not tied to a person (the events carry no user) and is not deduplicated: two clicks on one result are two clicks. (e) The retention of `analytics_events` was built by Step 5.4 PR B; the rule that decides whether the text of a global zero-result search may be kept is Step 7.4's (task "From Steps 5.1 and 5.2"). (f) **Review decisions:** the zero-result texts of the catalog are plaintext in `analytics_events` and the report lists them to every `analytics:view` holder: the write refuses an `@` and a run of seven digits in any script or width (NFKC), and a name typed in the catalog box can still get in; a minimum count before listing a text and a re-check at read time are Step 7.4's (task "From Steps 5.1 and 5.2"); the retention window was built by Step 5.4 PR B (#495). `passive` is chosen by the caller: search analytics are counts and hashes for the store's own report, not an audit trail of who searched (the audit log of Step 7.2 is), so a caller that skips them costs the report a row and nothing else. Clicks have an in-flight budget of their own, and a per-user limit on `POST /search/clicks` is Step 7.3's rate-limit work. The window of the report counts UTC days on `date`.
- [x] **QA fix `small-fixes-qa` (SRCH-040, accepted limit; rule 12).** A search of messages made only of Spanish stop words ("cuando", "mi") finds nothing: `websearch_to_tsquery('spanish', ...)` drops them and the query is empty. It is the dictionary's design and the message "¿Cuándo llega mi pedido?" is found by any other word of it ("llega"); a fallback to the `simple` configuration would index and rank every stop word of every message and was not built. Reconsider only if the owner asks for it, with Step 7.4. The notes OPS-SET-013 and OPS-SET-079 (an outbound webhook address typed with an IDN or with an upper-case host and a trailing dot is stored as typed) are not defects: every delivery parses the address again and checks `URL.hostname`, which is normalized, so nothing is bypassed; OPS-SET-414 (who holds `settings:edit` can lower the confirmations) is the owner's pending decision. **Debts of the same PR (rule 12), owner Step 7.3:** (a) a scheduled report saved with a fixed-offset time zone before this fix keeps running and is refused only when its zone is sent again: a sweep that lists them and asks their owners to pick a zone is not built; (b) `startsWith` filters over provider codes and guide prefixes (`carrier-connections.service.ts`, `carrier-status-mappings.service.ts`) do not escape `_` and `%`: the texts are written by the platform or a plugin manifest, not typed by a person, so the reach is one store's own rows, and a shared `likeContains`/`likeStartsWith` helper replaces the call sites when a third one is touched; (c) the empty `dateFormatConfirmed` of a bank import query is still a 400, like any other value that is not `true` or `false`; (d) the migration `order_tax_rounding` backfills the rounding of the books of that day into the orders that carry a tax snapshot (the rounding they were made with was never written down) and takes a lock on `orders` while it runs, like the other migrations of Step 7.3's maintenance-window note.
- [x] **Fix of the unit of the revenue (QA 2026-11-16, HC-010; rule 12 decisions and debts with their owners).** The rollup writes `orders.revenue` in whole units of the currency (`totalCents / 100`, from its first version in #485), the dashboard and the metrics of the plugins read it so, but the catalog declared it in cents and the files divided it by 100 again after a `Math.round`: 19.99 came out as `0.2` and one cent as `0` in the CSV, the spreadsheet, the PDF and the email of a scheduled report. **Decided:** one unit all the way, the one the dashboard already shows: `MetricUnits.CURRENCY` replaces `CENTS` (whole units of the currency), `displayValue` and `formatCell` do not divide, money is cut to the cent once, at the end, from the four decimals the rollup stores, and the header key is `unitCurrency` (es and en). **Rejected:** storing cents in the rollup (it matches the integer-money rule, but needs a migration of every stored row and a change of the dashboard and of the plugin API, which is the surface people already read). **No data to migrate:** every row of `metrics_hourly` and `metrics_daily` was written in units, so the stored figures are right and only the files were wrong. The two specs that held each half and contradicted each other (the rollup said dollars, the export seeded cents) now agree, and `tests/api/analytics-reports.spec.ts` has the case that crosses them: one order of 1999 cents and one of 1 cent through the rollup, the metrics route, the CSV, the spreadsheet and the PDF, all saying 19.99 and 0.01. **Left, each with its owner:** (a) the figure stays a decimal number (`Decimal(18,4)`), not integer cents: sums of units are exact only to four decimals, which is enough for a USD total but is not the integer-cents rule of the web; moving the rollup to integer cents is a decision for Step 7.4 with the migration it needs; (b) the CSV writes `20` and not `20.00` for a round amount (a number cell, so the spreadsheet formats it): a text cell with two decimals would be a choice for Step 7.4; (c) the unit label of money is the literal `USD` in the header of every file and the dashboard formats with USD, and the rollup sums `total_cents` of every order whatever its currency: the MVP has one currency (USD), and a store with another is Step 7.4's to decide; the email of a scheduled report shows money as `20.00` with no currency and no locale separators (Step 7.4); (d) three defects of the same QA pass that this PR leaves alone, to close in their own PRs under Step 7.3: a scheduled report in a zone ahead of UTC (or in UTC just after midnight) can go out before the UTC day it covers has closed and been rolled up, because its period is in UTC days but its hour is local and nothing checks the rollup (`report-schedule.ts` `reportPeriod`, `scheduled-report.runner.ts`); a weekly or monthly report is lost when the worker is down the whole day it falls due (`isReportDue`); and an order cancelled or adjusted after the two periods the rollup recomputes keeps counting in the revenue and the count of its day.
- [x] **Fix of the day of a scheduled report and of the late order (QA 2026-11-17, H-3, H-4, H-5; rule 12).** (H-3) A report was made from its hour by the clock of its zone, so a zone ahead of UTC (Auckland at hour 0) or UTC at 00:00-00:15 sent a period whose last UTC day was still running or not yet rolled up. **Decided:** the dispatcher queues a report only once the last UTC day of its period closed and the rollup had an hour to write it (`reportRollupReady`, `ReportLimits.ROLLUP_READY_GRACE_MS`); an idle day writes no row, so the check is by time and not by the existence of a row. (H-4) A weekly or monthly report was lost if the worker was down all day on its Monday or the 1st. **Decided:** `reportDueDay` owes the latest Monday or 1st at or before today, once the hour of today has come, and the job carries that day, so the period is the right one and `madeOnDay` stops a second send; one catch-up at most (a worker that was down for several periods sends the latest one), and a report is not owed for a period that ended before it was made (`createdAt`). A daily report keeps its rule (a missed day is not made up). (H-5) An order cancelled or adjusted after its day left the two-day recompute window kept that day's count and revenue for good. **Decided:** the daily run also queues, for every store, the UTC day of each order created within 90 days that changed in the last 48 hours (`RollupLimits.LATE_ORDER_*`, `enqueueLateDays`); the figure stays dated by when the order was made. **Rejected:** widening the window to N days (it recomputes every store N times a day and still freezes older days) and an adjustment posted on the day of the change (it makes the figure of a day depend on when people edit and needs a signed metric). **Debts:** (a) **owner question:** should revenue and the order count be dated by creation (today) or by cancellation; this PR keeps creation and corrects that day: Step 7.3; (b) an order changed by raw SQL that does not set `updated_at` is not seen: the three raw statements that exist (`customer-merge` sets it; conversation deletion and retention only clear `conversation_id`) move no figure; (c) an order changed more than 90 days after it was made stays as it was: Step 7.4 if the owner asks for it; (d) a report re-enabled after weeks sends the latest period owed once, which is the behavior wanted; (e) the rollup of a day that failed is not detected by the dispatcher (time only): a missing-rollup alarm is Step 7.3 (observability); (f) a daily report of a zone ahead of UTC is sent hours after its hour, when the rollup is ready; (g) the hourly rows (`metrics_hourly`) of an old order that changed are not rewritten, so an hourly view of an old range can differ from the daily one: Step 7.4 if the owner reads hours that far back; (h) the late-day scan filters `orders` by `updated_at` and `created_at` across stores once a day with no index on `updated_at`, and any edit of an order (a note, a tag) counts as a change: an `(updated_at)` index, or a `figures_changed_at` column set only on status and total changes, is Step 7.3 (database tuning); (i) a report is not marked as incomplete when the rollup jobs were delayed past the hour of grace: the missing-rollup alarm of (e).

### Step 5.3 — Caching and performance
Split into three PRs, all api, none stacked (owner's coordinator, 2026-11-14): **PR A** the cache and its invalidation, **PR B** the read replica routing, **PR C** PgBouncer and the cached reads that need new events.
- [x] Redis cache service with metrics and null sentinel. **`CacheService` (`libs/core/redis`) existed since Step 4.15 and Step 1.2** (hit and miss counters by namespace, a cached `null` is a hit, entries checked by a zod schema, scopes that drop a group of entries and protect a read that is loading, one load per key in flight, a Redis failure reads from the source); PR A names its `namespace` labels (`CacheNamespaces`) and its scopes (`CacheScopes`) in `libs/core/platform/cache/cache-keys.ts`, with the storeId in every key and scope.
- [x] Complete cache invalidation listener. **PR A (`apps/api/src/modules/cache`, `CacheInvalidationListener`):** the services announce the change with a domain event after the commit and the listener moves the scope: `TAG_*`, `SNIPPET_*` and `STORE_SETTINGS_UPDATED` (now emitted by `TagsService`, `SnippetsService` and `PreferencesService`, with payloads in `event-payloads.ts`) drop the store's tag list, snippet list and preferences, which are now cached for `CacheTTL.MEDIUM`; `tests/api/settings-cache.spec.ts` proves it (a row edited behind the api's back is still served from the cache, a change through the api shows at once, a change in one store never reaches the cache of another, and mutating the listener or the key makes it fail). Measured with a throwaway script (the k6 suite of Step 7.7 is deferred): 72 requests of three people on seeded data gave a hit rate of 95.1% (tenant context 95.8%, tags 93.3%, snippets 96.7%, preferences 90.0%; 94.3% for the three new reads alone), over the 40% of the Done when. **Left for PR C (rule 12) — PR C decided, and moved it to Step 7.4 (task "From Step 5.3 (PR C)" there):** (a) the cached reads of `TDD_08 §1.4` that PR A did not touch, each needing its events first: `conversation.counts` (the archive, spam, snooze and bulk sweeps publish no event the listener could hear), `customer.byIdentity` and `channel.connection` (written by the worker's inbound pipeline: their events must be in `BridgedEvents` for an api listener to hear them, or the key needs a short TTL only), `product.search` (`PRODUCT_*` and `INVENTORY_MOVED` exist; add the case when search results are cached); (b) `TenantContextService.invalidateUser/invalidateStore` are still called by the services that change a membership or a role: move them behind `MEMBER_*` and `ROLE_UPDATED` events when those are emitted; (c) the readers of `StoreSettings` that go straight to the database (`orders`, `returns`, `widget`, the worker) are not cached: PR C decides, with the same listener, which of them is hot enough. **Test convention (found when CI went red on the first push):** the builders of `tests/builders` write as the owner, with no event, so the ones that write a cached table (`createTag`, `createSnippet`, `resetStoreSettings`, and any suite that writes `StoreSettings.preferences` by hand) call `dropCachedSettings` (`tests/builders/cache.ts`), which does what the listener does; the next cached read added to this step must add its scope there. **Accepted limits:** a Redis failure while a change is announced leaves the old entry for at most its TTL (five minutes for these three), and is logged at error level by the event emitter (which suppresses listener errors by default), with no retry; a read that was already loading in this process when a change commits is shared with the next read of the same key (`CacheService` joins loads in flight and an invalidation does not clear them), so that one answer can be the old one: PR C may key the loads by generation if the k6 run shows it matters; `STORE_SETTINGS_UPDATED` is emitted only by `PreferencesService`, so the inbox, inventory, returns and carrier settings that also write `StoreSettings` need their own event before any reader of them is cached; the L1 in-process cache of `TDD_08 §1.1` is not built, because nothing the MVP holds is read on every request, global and rarely changed (platform settings and feature flags are trimmed, `MVP_TRIM_CHECKLIST.md`).
- [x] Read replica routing through the extension. **PR B:** `PrismaService.replica()` already exists (`@prisma/extension-read-replicas`, answers from the primary when `DATABASE_REPLICA_URL` is not set) and no service calls it yet; PR B moves the reads that tolerate lag (analytics, exports, search, list views of `TDD_08 §2.5`) to it, keeps every read-then-write and every guard on the primary, adds a test with a second database that proves a list goes to the replica and a write path does not, and a check that stops a new `replica()` call in a write path. **Built in PR B:** (1) a defect of the wiring, fixed: `@prisma/extension-read-replicas` sends EVERY read of the extended client to the replica when there is one, not only what asks for `$replica()`, so with `DATABASE_REPLICA_URL` set the guards, the tenant context and every read-then-write would have read the replica; `PrismaService.client` is now `$primary()` (one object, which `afterCommit` tells apart by identity) and `replica()` is the only way to the replica; (2) the reads that go to it: the dashboard metrics (`MetricsQueryService`) and the report of searches (`SearchReportService`, both statements from one reader). **Every search stays on the primary (decision of the review, high lens):** the global, message, customer, order and product searches apply erasure, deleted messages, hidden conversations and assignment, which a lagging replica would show through for a moment, and the pickers copy a price from the product search; the TDD's "search uses the replica" waits for the same read-your-writes rule as the lists; `foldInDatabase` and `readMetricBuckets` take a `SqlReader` (`Pick<client, '$queryRaw'>`) so the caller picks the source (the worker's report keeps the primary); (3) `tests/api/read-replica-routing.spec.ts` runs the real app against a second database (`<test database>_replica`, created and migrated by `ensureReplicaDatabase`, which nothing replicates into): the replica holds no member and no role, so a guard that read it answers 403; it proves the metrics and the report of searches answer from the replica, and the search, the product list and a PATCH answer from the primary; (4) `pnpm validate:replica` (`scripts/check-replica-routing.ts`, CI job `lint-and-types-checks` and pre-push) fails on a `replica()` call outside the files of `scripts/replica-readers.ts`, in a guard or an interceptor, in a `@Post/@Put/@Patch/@Delete` route, or in a function that also writes, locks or opens a transaction, and on a listed file that no longer calls it. **Left (rule 12), owner Step 7.4:** the list views of `TDD_08 §2.5` (conversations, customers, orders, products, inventory, exports, scheduled reports, `my-performance`) stay on the primary on purpose: the web refetches them right after a write and a replica a moment behind would show the old row. They move behind a read-your-writes rule (a short-lived per-store marker of the last write that sends the read to the primary, or a lag check) and one at a time; `DATABASE_REPLICA_URL` is not set in any environment until then, so nothing changes in production, and the api's `DATABASE_REPLICA_URL` must never be set without the replica being fed by streaming replication. The worker is given `DATABASE_REPLICA_URL` by `HttpPlatformModule` like the api (a second idle pool) but never calls `replica()`: its reads stay on the primary. **Accepted (second review pass):** the report of searches may miss the person's own last searches for the replication lag, and its two statements are the same replica but not one snapshot; the check `validate:replica` looks at the function that holds the call (a write done by a helper is for the review), and `replica()` returns the full client type (a read-only type would force raw SQL everywhere; the AST check and a real replica's read-only transaction stop a write). **Accepted:** a dashboard figure (replica) and the same figure in a scheduled report (primary, worker) can differ by the replication lag until the replica is fed.
- [x] PgBouncer configuration verified end to end. **Built in PR C:** (1) `docker-compose.yml`: the `pgbouncer` service carries every setting of `TDD_08 §2.6` (transaction mode, `max_client_conn` 1000, `default_pool_size` 25, `reserve_pool_size` 5, `reserve_pool_timeout` 3, `server_idle_timeout` 600, `max_db_connections` 100, `ignore_startup_parameters`, `scram-sha-256`); with no database in its `DATABASE_URL` the image writes a wildcard entry, so the test database goes through it as well as `platform_dev` (`AUTH_DBNAME=platform_dev`: the `user_lookup` function lives only there), `STATS_USERS=pgbouncer` lets the monitoring role read `SHOW POOLS`, and Postgres starts with `max_connections=250` because `max_db_connections` counts per database (two behind the wildcard, up to 200 backends) and migrations and the owner connect beside it; the password of the `pgbouncer` role comes from `PGBOUNCER_AUTH_PASSWORD` (compose default is the dev value, as for the other dev passwords; `.env.example` and `scripts/db-role-env.ts` declare it, `validate:env` checks them). `DATABASE_URL` through PgBouncer and `DIRECT_DATABASE_URL` for migrations were already the rule of `.env.example` and `prisma.config.ts`. (2) `TEST_POOLER_URL` (`connectionUrls()` in `libs/core/database/testing`, local hosts only) sends the app URLs of the api and worker roles through the pooler while the owner stays direct. (3) `pnpm test:pooler` (`tests/jest.pooler.config.cts`): `tests/pooler/pgbouncer-pooling.spec.ts` reads `SHOW CONFIG` (the TDD settings), proves with `SHOW POOLS` that 40 clients shared at most 30 backends and some waited, that a client's next transaction is served by a different backend (why the tenant settings are `set_config(..., true)`), that a transaction-local setting does not reach the next client and that an advisory lock holds across clients; beside it run the tenant isolation suite and the specs that reach `lockStoreForWrite`, `lockStoreScope`, the advisory locks of the worker services and the tenant transaction (`customers-store-lock`, `orders`, `transfers`, `settings`, `inventory-engine`, `orders-lifecycle`, `remittances`, `carrier-event-processing`, `analytics-rollups`; 920 tests passed through the pooler on a laptop; a new spec that takes such a lock is added to `tests/jest.pooler.config.cts`). CI job `pooler-tests` (the compose stack; it also runs the `core-database` integration suites through the pooler, which cover the worker role and the lock timeout of the api role). Mutation: with the pooler in session mode, the settings, the sharing and the different-backend cases fail. **Owner, pending: add `pooler-tests` to the required checks of the `main` ruleset** once it has run once on GitHub (the job is not required until the owner decides).

### Step 5.6 — Integration plugins (runtime)

In the v1.2 MVP the platform runs third-party and private integration plugins (for example
the owner's own POS or inventory app, or a Shopify connector later). The marketplace, its
review queue and revenue sharing stay deferred (`TDD_10 §8`). Builds on Step 5.4 (webhook
delivery, SSRF protection, key hashing) and Step 1.0 (queues).
**Division into PRs (coordinator, 2026-11-15).** The step ships as 19 PRs, none stacked: "depends on" means it starts with that PR merged
and `main` up to date. Each task below ends with the PR (or PRs) that owns it and its wave; the task boxes stay where they are and are
checked by the PR that closes them. Every PR keeps to about 40 files, api before web, and writes in this step the debt it leaves.
Security, tenancy and migration PRs (P1, P2, P3, M1, C1, C2, C3, E1, E2) are reviewed at the high level and repeated until a pass
returns fewer than 10 findings. The PRs that expose routes (M1, E1 to E7) each add their scopes to `PluginScopes` and
`PluginScopePermissions`, map their routes in `scripts/plugin-api-coverage-map.ts` and lower `scripts/plugin-api-baseline.json` with
`--update-down`; they touch the same four files, so a conflict of lines is expected and is resolved keeping both sides.

| S1 | sdk-audit | audit that the SDK is aligned with the core, and the check that keeps it so | none | 0 |

Waves: 0 (P1, S1 in parallel) then 1 (P2 and C1 in parallel) then 2 (P3, M1, E1 to E7, C2 and C3: all independent of each other)
then 3 (C4, W1, W2). The critical path is P1, P2, C1/C2/C3, C4. No more than two heavy sessions at a time.

An organization registers at most `PluginRegistrationLimits.MAX_PER_ORGANIZATION` (50), under a row lock of the organization. (2) The job id of an inbound event is `inboundJobId(pluginId, event)` (the plugin and the connection id), not the installation id the text of `§6.7.5` named: an account belongs to one store and one installation (`@@unique([pluginId, connectionId])`), so the two keys tell the same events apart and the one that already serves the official channels needs no second function; the text of the TDD now says so. (3) A file address is judged at the door by its shape only (`isWellFormedPublicHttpsUrl`: https, default port, no credentials, no private name or address literal) and never resolved by the api: the api never opens it, so a hostile plugin cannot make the api resolve names (up to 50 per request); the fetch resolves, checks every address and pins the connection, and that is where DNS rebinding is closed; rejected: resolving at the door too (the spec's "checked when the event arrives" is met by the shape check, and a second resolution would only add a cost an attacker controls). - [x] Install flow: consent screen, webhook-endpoint challenge with `assertPublicHttpsUrl`, `PluginInstallation` in `PENDING_SETUP`, scoped API key stored as prefix and sha256 hash only, one-time setup code (5 minutes, Redis) exchanged for the key, then `ACTIVE` **(PR P2, wave 1)**
  - **Built in PR P2:** `GET /plugins/:id/consent` (`SETTINGS_MANAGE_PLUGINS`; the plugin id) returns what installing would grant, read again from the stored manifest: scopes, what is new against the installation of the store (`newScopes`), the rate limit, the webhook endpoint and events, the legal links and the settings url. `POST /plugins/install` takes `scopes` for an integration plugin: they must be exactly the ones the manifest asks for now (`PLUGIN_CONSENT_MISMATCH`, 409, when the manifest changed after the screen). Then the webhook endpoint gets the challenge (`PluginChallengeService`: a POST with a fresh 256-bit value through `pinnedHttpsExchange`, which resolves the name, connects only to the address it checked, follows no redirect and reads at most 1 KiB; the plugin must echo the value in a JSON answer; `PLUGIN_CHALLENGE_FAILED`, 412), and the installation is written in `PENDING_SETUP` with its scopes, the endpoint that passed (`PluginInstallation.webhookEndpoint`, migration `plugin_installation_endpoint` with rollback) and the rate limit of the manifest. The answer carries the one-time setup code (43 characters, 256 bits, five minutes, Redis under its SHA-256, one live code per installation: a new one voids the old) and the settings url; `POST /plugins/:id/setup-code` (the installation's id) issues a new one while the installation is waiting. `POST /plugin-api/setup/exchange` (public, body `{ code }`, `no-store`, per-address limit of the public profile) reads and removes the code in one Redis command, makes the key (`plg_live_` + 256 bits), stores only its first 12 characters and its SHA-256, and sets `ACTIVE` in one transaction under the store lock; the key is returned in that answer and never again (the audit entries carry neither the code nor the key). One answer (`PLUGIN_SETUP_CODE_INVALID`, 401) for a code that is unknown, expired, used, or whose installation is no longer waiting. An installation that is `ACTIVE` and meets a newer manifest takes the new scopes (and passes the challenge again if the endpoint changed) through the same install call with the new consent, keeps its key, and audits `plugin.scopes_updated`; revoking voids a waiting code; installing again after a revocation resets the installation to `PENDING_SETUP` with no key.

(b) the exchange is a public route of the plugin API (no key yet; the code is the credential), a case that rule 5 of `CLAUDE.md` does not list: `TDD_10 §6.3` requires it, and the owner adds it to that list; (c) the catalog entry does not say that an installation is waiting for its plugin (`installed` is true only when `ACTIVE`): PR W1 adds `installationStatus` to the entry and draws the pending state, the consent screen and the "new code" button; (d) revoking keeps the hash of the key and relies on the status check of the guard (immediate, no cache): PR P3 clears it and sends the final `plugin.revoked`; (e) there is no "regenerate the key" for an active installation: a lost key is a revoke and a new install (PR P3 with the revocation, or Phase 2); (f) the worker's `pinnedHttpsPost` and `pinnedHttpsGet` and the new `pinnedHttpsExchange` (libs/core/url-safety) repeat the same pinned-request recipe (agent, lookup, servername): PR P3 extracts one shared `pinnedRequestOptions` helper, delivers plugin webhooks through `pinnedHttpsExchange` and moves the worker's tenant webhooks onto it in the same PR; (i) a plugin key refused for lack of scope or permission is logged (installation, kind, what was missing) and not audited or counted as `PermissionGuard` does for a person: PR P3 adds the audit entry and the metric with the revocation work; (g) the plugin routes sit under the default per-address limit of the other routes, plus the per-installation limit of the guard: there is no per-user limit of the settings writes to share (debt (k) of PR P1 closes here as stated); (h) a webhook endpoint that answers the challenge is trusted by its address: it is not re-challenged on every delivery (PR P3 resolves it again at each delivery, `assertPublicHttpsUrl`).

  - **Built in PR P2 (the guard and the rate limit):** `PluginApiKeyGuard` (`apps/api/src/modules/plugins/plugin-api-key.guard.ts`) takes the place of the three global guards on a route marked `@PluginApi(...scopes)` (public for them): the key is found by its hash and refused with one answer (`PLUGIN_API_KEY_INVALID`, 401) when it is missing, is a store key (`pk_live_`), is unknown, or its installation is not `ACTIVE` or its plugin not `APPROVED` (so revoking or suspending stops it at the next call); the installation's own limit (`rateLimitPerMinute`) is counted in Redis through the throttler storage, answers 429 with the time to wait and refuses the call when Redis fails; every scope the route names must be granted (`PLUGIN_SCOPE_DENIED`, 403); every `@RequirePermissions` / `@RequireAnyPermission` of the route must be inside the permissions of the granted scopes (`PERMISSION_DENIED`, 403); and the request gets `store`, `organization`, `permissions` and `pluginInstallation` (never `user`): the store is the one of the installation row, which belongs to exactly one store, and nothing the call carries changes it. `GET /plugin-api/installation` (no scope) says who the key is. A route that lists no scopes is a mistake and is refused. The controllers of M1 and E1 to E7 use `@PluginApi(...)` and `@CurrentStore()` as in `tests/api/plugin-install.spec.ts`.
- [ ] **Messages from a plugin, with the author and the quiet mode chosen by the plugin (owner, 2026-10-29; Crisp's plugin API lets the plugin choose how a message looks):** `POST /plugin-api/messages` (`messages:write`) sends a reply or an internal note to a conversation. It takes: `type` (`text`, `note` or a file type with the media of Step 3.4: uploaded through the API, scanned, and sent with its text as the caption; a note carries no files in the MVP); `authorType`, `system` (the default) or `agent`; `userId`, required with `agent` (an active member of the store; the message is theirs, with their own name and avatar); `quiet` (default false); an optional `nickname` (cut to a length, control characters removed; the plugin's name by default) and an optional avatar (never a remote url: the icon of the plugin, and the plugin's own image once Step 3.4 stores it), both only for `system`. **The author and `quiet` are separate choices** (`authorType` is its own column), so a plugin can send as `system` quietly, as `system` and raise the chat, or as an agent in any of the two ways. **Author:** `system` never counts as a human answer: `recordReply` does not set `firstResponseAt` for it (that date feeds the first response time of `TDD_11 §7.2`, and an automatic answer would make it look instant) and it sets `Conversation.firstAutomatedResponseAt` instead (new nullable column, once; migration with its rollback script), so that automation is measured on its own and never hides how long the team takes. `agent` counts as that person's answer, as if they had written it. Answering does not take a conversation out of the pending queue or stop a response SLA: only an explicit resolve does, and a plugin with `conversations:write` can resolve its own. **`quiet`** (core: `CreateMessageBody.quiet`, `MessagesService.create` and `ConversationsService.recordReply`): the customer gets the message and the open thread and the preview of the list show it in real time, but the conversation does not change at all: `lastMessageAt` stays (the order of the list stays), it is not reopened, and `lastOutboundAt`, `firstResponseAt` and `firstAutomatedResponseAt` are not touched. Without `quiet` a reply moves and reopens the conversation like an agent's. A note changes nothing in the conversation, as today. `quiet` is for plugins only in the MVP (no checkbox for agents) and the send is subject to the messaging window of the channel like any other. **Trace:** two new columns of `Message`, in one migration with its rollback script: `authorPluginId` (the plugin that wrote it, always, whichever the author) and `authorNickname`; `MessageView` returns both, and the "automatic" mark and "sent through <plugin>" of Step 3.2 are drawn here, once a message can carry them (decided 2026-10-30). Every plugin message is audited with the plugin as the actor. There is no `from: user`: a plugin cannot write as the customer. Tests: a quiet reply leaves `lastMessageAt`, status, `lastOutboundAt`, `firstResponseAt` and `firstAutomatedResponseAt` as they were; a `system` reply never sets `firstResponseAt`; an `agent` reply does; `agent` with a user of another store or with no `userId` is refused; a plugin without `messages:write` gets 403; isolation case **(PR M1, wave 2)**

- [x] **PR W1-2 (wave 3; server and web, decided 2026-11-16, rule 12):** delete a plugin the organization registered (debt (a) of PR W1, (h) of PR P1, (f) of PR P3). `DELETE /plugins/:id` (`plugins.byId`, `SETTINGS_MANAGE_PLUGINS`, `TDD_10 §6.1`) with the name typed in the body; the catalog entry carries `registered` (the organization's own manifest) and Settings → Plugins draws a Delete button on such a row that holds no installation, through `DELETE_PLUGIN` (critical tier, the name is the phrase). `PluginDeletionService`: 404 for a plugin of another organization, an official one or none (before the name is looked at); 400 `PLUGIN_DELETE_NOT_CONFIRMED`; 409 `PLUGIN_IN_USE` while any store holds an installation that is not revoked, a revoked one that still has its webhook endpoint or secret, or one with channel connections; otherwise the plugin and its revoked installations are removed in one transaction under the organization lock of a registration, audited as `plugin.deleted`, the icon of a channel plugin is removed and the remote registry refreshed. No schema change, so no migration. Tests: `tests/api/plugin-delete.spec.ts`, the `plugin` case of the isolation matrix now also tries the delete as a stranger (a mutant that drops the organization filter of the lookup fails it), `plugins-requests.spec.ts`, and the e2e step "deletes the plugin only with its name typed".
  - **Decisions:** (1) physical delete, not a mark: the id is free again and nothing in the catalog has to filter a state; the alternative (a `deleted` status that keeps the id owned by the organization) was rejected because it touches every catalog query and the registration rules for a case the audit log already covers; (2) the name is the phrase (`phraseMatches`: space around it is not an error, the case is), the word `REVOKE` of the revocation is not reused so that a habit cannot delete; (3) the body is optional in the schema and checked in the service, so that a stranger gets the same 404 whether or not a name is sent (a required body would answer 400 before the organization is checked, which the isolation matrix could not tell from a pass); (4) a revoked installation that still holds its endpoint or secret blocks the delete: the worker still has a last `plugin.revoked` delivery to sign with it.
  - **Left by PR W1-2, each with its owner:** (a) closed by fix N-A7-08 (below); (b) what the plugin wrote keeps its id and the messages name it by id once it is gone, and another organization may register the same id later (its own catalog names it for its own stores only, nothing crosses organizations): accepted, no tombstone; (c) the Delete button is drawn from the catalog of the store of the request, which does not say that a sibling store still holds the plugin: the api answers 409 and the toast says so; a count of the stores that hold it is Step 7.4 with the visual pass; (d) an install that races the deletion of the same plugin can answer a 500 from the foreign key (the delete itself answers 409 in the opposite order): Step 7.3, with the install taking a row lock; (e) the Delete button is in the row only, not in the detail dialog; (f) the delete needs `SETTINGS_MANAGE_PLUGINS` in the store of the request, not in every store: it removes the revoked installations (and their delivery log) of sibling stores and its 409 tells a manager something of them, as the catalog and the registration are already the organization's (an organization-level permission waits for the roles of Step 7.4); (g) `plugin-delete.spec.ts`, the unit specs and the e2e step run in CI only: no browser here.
  - **Fix N-A7-08 (ARREGLOS-1, rule 12):** a channel plugin whose revoked installation holds connections could never be deleted and kept counting against the 50 of the organization. `DELETE /plugins/:id` now **archives** it in that case: `Plugin.status = 'archived'` (a new `PluginStatus`, no migration: the column is a string; no rollback needed), audited as `plugin.archived`. Every reader already filters on `approved`, so it leaves the catalog, the install flows and the remote registry; the registration limit counts only the rest; its installations, connections and conversations stay. A DELETE of an archived plugin answers 404 and registering its id again answers the usual 409 (the row keeps the id for the history it holds, for the organization and for any other: this narrows debt (b), where another organization may register the id of a plugin that was deleted, not archived). The archive locks the plugin row first and an integration or remote-channel install takes it `FOR SHARE` in its write (so an install cannot commit on a plugin archived meanwhile; the same lock closes debt (d) for those installs, the install of an official channel never meets a deletable plugin). Still 409 `PLUGIN_IN_USE` while an installation is not revoked or has its last webhook pending. **Rejected:** a `deleted_at` column (migration, and every query would need the filter that `status` already gives); freeing the id on archive (the conversations would then name another organization's plugin). **Left:** (1) reactivating an archived plugin (not asked, the owner registers a new id): Step 7.4; (2) purging the history of an archived plugin after a retention period: Step 7.3, with the retention of conversations.

### Step 5.7 — Plugin widgets

## Milestone 7 — Production readiness

### Step 7.1 — Security hardening
- [x] **Lock timeout of the api (QA, 2026-11-07; the base blocked for 25 s left every request waiting):** the role `platform_app` gives up after `ApiLockTimeout` (5 s, under the 15 s of a tenant transaction) through `ALTER ROLE ... IN DATABASE ... SET lock_timeout` (migration `20261113120000_api_lock_timeout`, rollback beside it; a role setting and not `SET`, which `TDD_01 §3.2` forbids through PgBouncer). The api answers `503 DATABASE_BUSY` with `retryAfterSeconds` (`isLockTimeoutError`, `GlobalExceptionFilter`; a warning, not a Sentry event). **Rollout:** a connection already open keeps the old setting, so restart the api (and PgBouncer's server connections) after the migration. **Left on purpose, owner Step 7.1:** (1) `statement_timeout` for the api (a runaway query still holds a connection; needs the slowest real query measured first, then a value above it); (2) the worker has no lock timeout: its jobs are long and retried, decide per job with the measures of Step 7.3; (3) `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`; (4) the web draws `DATABASE_BUSY` with a generic message and no retry button; (5) no metric counts these timeouts (the log line is all there is); (6) **the web retries a 503**: `shouldRetry` in `apps/web/lib/query-client.ts` retries every 5xx twice, so a blocked table makes each page view hold up to three connections for 5 s each: skip `DATABASE_BUSY` there and honor `retryAfterSeconds` (a web task; the inbox bundle has little room, measure it) **Done in PR `fix/web-no-retry-database-busy`:** a busy database is tried once more (not twice) after the wait the api asks for (`retryDelayOf`, up to 30 s), through `ClientErrorCodes.DATABASE_BUSY`; only reads are tried again (a mutation never is: a write sent again blind can repeat its effects), and a query that sets its own `retry` does not get the rule, and none does today; (7) the 503 is mapped only by the HTTP filter: a lock timeout in the websocket gateway, a bridged event handler or a cron that runs as `platform_app` surfaces as an error log; (8) **the migration needs the privilege to alter `platform_app`** (the one that created the role has it); on a server where infrastructure provisioned the role, grant it or run the `ALTER ROLE` once by hand, and the deploy docs of Step 7.5 must say so.
- [x] Helmet on the API, CSP in Next with per-store plugin origins (api: `libs/core/http/src/security-headers.ts`, helmet with the frame and opener headers written down; web: nonce CSP in `proxy.ts`, `frame-src` per store from the cookie, `X-Frame-Options: DENY` and `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin` in `STATIC_SECURITY_HEADERS`; the directive specs and `apps/web-e2e/specs/security-headers.spec.ts` pin them on a real page). **Left on purpose:** (a) no `report-uri`/`report-to`: there is no endpoint to receive reports, and Sentry's CSP report URL is tied to its project, so it waits for the Sentry setup of Step 7.3; (b) the grade A of securityheaders.com can only be checked against a deployed host: Step 7.3 (`docs/IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md` deploy checks)
- [x] Rate limiting, application (Redis) (PR #867, rule 12). What already stood: the per-address default (`ThrottleProfiles.DEFAULT`, 100/min, Redis storage of our own, `ResilientThrottlerGuard` that fails open and logs), the `PUBLIC`, magic-link, invitation, webhook, plugin-api and enumeration profiles, `@UserRateLimit` for search and the customer list, `TRUST_PROXY_HOPS`, and the `platform_rate_limit_hits_total` metric. The real hole was that an authenticated person had **no budget of their own**: only the per-address one, so one stolen or scripted token used from many addresses was never counted as one. Added `AuthenticatedUserRateLimitGuard` (`libs/core/http/src/throttler`, registered by `TenancyModule` first of the three tenancy guards, right after `AuthGuard`, so `request.user` is known and a refusal by the store or the permission is counted): every route behind `AuthGuard` spends `AuthenticatedUserRateLimit` (`libs/core/domain/auth/auth-constants.ts`, 600 a minute per user id, counter `user:authenticated`), on top of the per-address layer and of any `@UserRateLimit` profile of the route (a different counter). A request with no user (public routes, probes, the plugin api, which has the limit of its installation) is not counted by it. It fails open and logs when Redis is down, like the other layers; a refusal is a 429 with `Retry-After` and adds to the metric. Spec: `authenticated-user-rate-limit.guard.spec.ts` (unit) and `authenticated-user-rate-limit.spec.ts` (a person past the budget is refused from many addresses, another person is not, a request with no person is not counted). **Left on purpose:** (a) the per-address default stays at 100/min for every route, so several agents behind one office address still share it: raising it relaxes the posture of the whole API and is **owner-only** (decide with the real office address and `rate_limit_exceeded` per route in Grafana; the per-user budget above is what makes raising it safe); (b) 600 is a ceiling chosen above the web's real use and not measured: tune it from the metric in Step 7.3; (c) the per-user layer is not keyed by store or plugin installation (the plugin api keeps its own key limit); a per-store budget waits for a second store of the owner to need it. (d) accepted trade-off (review): the counter is one per user id with no exemption, so whoever holds a stolen token can burn the 600 a minute from several addresses and make the person's own calls, logout and revoke included, answer 429 until the window ends; a small separate counter for logout and session revoke closes it, owner Step 7.3. (e) the guard is registered right after `AuthGuard` and before `TenantGuard`, so a refusal by the store or the permission spends the budget; the real order and the Redis storage are driven by `tests/api/authenticated-user-rate-limit.spec.ts` (600 refused store calls, then the 429); the shared test app (`tests/helpers/app.ts`) turns this guard off for the other suites, which make hundreds of calls as a few users, as they dodge the per-address limit with a fresh address. (h) the browser suite signs in as a few people for hundreds of calls a minute (every page polls) and got 429 on the real budget, so `playwright.shared.ts` starts the api with `E2E_USER_RATE_LIMIT` (100000, `NODE_ENV=test` only, raise-only and bounded like `E2E_MAGIC_LINK_LIMIT`; the performance run keeps the real one). (f) the per-user and per-address layers wait on Redis with no command timeout, so a hung Redis (not a failed one) stalls the api; a timeout on the throttler storage covers both, Step 7.3. (g) routes with no `request.user` and no limit of their own (a store API key, if one is added) have only the per-address layer.
- [ ] Rate limiting, edge (Cloudflare rules): **owner-only**. `TDD_05 §3.3` lists three rules (login brute force 5/min per IP, API flood 1000/min per IP with a managed challenge, widget flood 120/min per IP) to be created in the Cloudflare dashboard of the real zone, which is an account the repository has no access to. Nothing to build here: the owner creates them when the public hostnames are proxied (`TDD_05 §4`), and the application layer above holds meanwhile.

  - The roles `platform_app` (subject to RLS, used by `apps/api`) and `platform_worker` (`BYPASSRLS`, used by `apps/worker`, which also processes every inbound channel event) already exist since Step 0.4, and the services already connect with them; this step only turns the policies on
  - `scripts/rls.sql`, generated from the schema, with `ENABLE` + `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` and one policy per table: tables with `store_id` use `app.store_ids`; the organization-scoped inventory tables (`warehouses`, `stock_transfers`, `stock_counts`) use `app.organization_ids`; `store_warehouses` uses its `store_id`; child tables (messages, order items, transfer and count lines, allocations, movements) follow their parent. The `audit_logs` grants already exist since Step 0.4
  - Identity and bootstrap tables are NOT under RLS, because the guards read them before any tenant context exists: `users`, `sessions`, `verification_tokens`, `invitations`, `organizations`, `stores`, `memberships` and `roles`. They stay protected by code (user id or token) and by the isolation suite
  - **The mechanism is already chosen and was verified by a spike** (2026-10-24, `TDD_01 §3.2`): one interactive transaction per unit of work with `set_config(..., true)` as its first statement, kept in an `AsyncLocalStorage`, with `PrismaService.client` returning that transaction and `PrismaService.transaction(fn)` joining it. The per-operation extension was rejected because it breaks atomicity. This step implements it and re-runs the same checks as tests: atomic rollback, no cross-tenant leak under concurrency through PgBouncer, raw SQL (`SearchService`), parallel queries on one transaction, and row locks (`TDD_16 §4.2`)
  - **Tenant interceptor:** after `TenantGuard`, a `TenantContextInterceptor` runs the whole handler inside `PrismaService.tenantTransaction(ctx, fn)`, which sets `app.store_ids` and `app.organization_ids` with `set_config(..., true)` (never the session-level form; a lint rule forbids `false`) and applies explicit `maxWait` and `timeout` limits. The `await` of every query stays inside the scope, and **no external I/O runs inside it** (carrier, channel, S3 and e-mail calls are queued and run in the worker). `TenantGuard` fills the context from the caller's memberships; plugin API requests set only the installation's store; widget requests set only the store of the site key's connection; requests with no context see no rows. Streaming endpoints and the WebSocket gateway use an explicit `TenantContext` instead of the interceptor
  - **API code that runs outside a tenant request fails loudly instead of returning empty results:** the WebSocket gateway, domain-event listeners fed by the events bridge (notifications, plugin webhooks), and the public endpoints must either run inside an explicit `TenantContext.run({ storeIds, organizationIds }, fn)` taken from the event payload or the verified credential, or hand the work to the worker. In the `api` process a query on a store-scoped table with no context throws in dev, test and CI
  - **Pre-context lookups** (widget site key to store, plugin API key hash to installation, tenant API key hash to store, a carrier webhook's connection id to its store) use small `SECURITY DEFINER` SQL functions that `platform_app` may call and that return only the store id. A globally unique value that belongs to another store (a `ChannelConnection` `(pluginId, connectionId)`) is detected from the unique violation, never by reading the other store's row

Original text: the bulk `MARK_READ` of up to 500 conversations does about six extra round trips each (about 1.5 to 3 s more) inside the one 15 s tenant transaction, and a timeout rolls back the whole batch of 500. Fix: one batched lookup after the loop (latest customer message per conversation, one read of `sendReadReceipts`), then the receipts and emits after the commit. Known limit: one failed lookup loses the receipts of the whole batch (the reads stand; a warn with the size is logged); a customer message that arrives after the batch began and before its conversation is marked read is cleared as read but gets no receipt (the cutoff is the start of the batch; the next read of that conversation tells it), and `created_at` comes from the clock that wrote the row, the cutoff from the database clock (skew tolerance of the two). The cutoff travels as the text the database gave (`clock_timestamp() AT TIME ZONE 'UTC'`), never as a `Date`, and if that read fails the batch sends no receipts (warn with the size; fail closed). The column holds UTC wall time (written by the Prisma client), so the activation runbook should check `SHOW timezone` of the app connections. Done in the same branch: the cases of (b) with the CI database (a lookup that fails in the database keeps the reads; no receipt for a plugin reader, one for a person: `tests/api/bulk-mark-read-receipts.spec.ts`), the `ROUND_ROBIN_TO_TEAM` case under enforcement, and the check of `SHOW timezone` in `docs/RLS_ACTIVATION_RUNBOOK.md`. The api (`MagicLinkService`) queues `REQUEST_MAGIC_LINK` there, and `MagicLinkIssuer` queues the `SEND_EMAIL` of the link there. The sealed invitation outbox (#889, #900) is untouched: it stays on `email` through `EmailProcessor`, and `AuthEmailProcessor` refuses `DELIVER_INVITATION_EMAIL` (spec). **Rollout and rollback:** deploy the worker before the api. A worker without `AuthEmailProcessor` (the api went out first, or the worker was rolled back) leaves the jobs of the new api waiting in `auth-email` and nothing alerts: the requests answer 202 and no email arrives until a worker that consumes the queue runs again, and each stranded job then voids the link of the one before it, so only the last link of an address works (the links live 15 minutes, so a long outage means asking again). That is why the alert on the age of the oldest job (c) matters and why a rollback of the worker must roll the api back with it. `EmailProcessor` still serves a `REQUEST_MAGIC_LINK` that an api of the previous release queued on `email`. **Timing (#43):** the answer of the request is uniform by construction (the api counts the limit and queues one job for any address and never looks the address up; the worker does) and is proved by the structural spec and the measured one (`magic-link.service.integration.spec`, 300 pairs interleaved, tolerance of the spread of the samples); nothing changed there. **Decisions (rule 12):** (1) the refusal of a link is not audited: an unknown, used or expired link has no user or store to attribute it to, and an audit row per refusal would be a write an anonymous caller makes at will; the answer is already the same for unknown and used links, the consume route has the per-IP limit of `MagicLinkThrottle` (429 after the limit, proved in `auth.controller.integration.spec`), and a link is 256 bits, so probing the tokens of other accounts is bounded by that limit and is not feasible; the request path writes no audit row for a known or an unknown address alike, so the negation is uniform; (2) no priority inside the general queue: a queue of its own isolates the failure and the limiter, and priorities do not. **Left (rule 12):** (a) remove the `REQUEST_MAGIC_LINK` case of `EmailProcessor` one release after worker and api run this code, and only after confirming that the `email` queue holds no `REQUEST_MAGIC_LINK` job (waiting, delayed or failed) in the deployed environment: owner Step 7.3-B; (b) re-run the HTTP probe (60 requests of each kind, median and p95) against the staging deploy to confirm the gap is gone: owner Step 7.5 (needs staging); until then the gap is proved by the structural and the measured specs against a local Redis, not against a deployment; (c) a metric and an alert on the age of the oldest job of `auth-email`, so a stopped consumer is seen: Step 7.4 observability; (e) the `SEND_EMAIL` job of the link holds the raw link (and the address) in Redis while it waits or is retried, unsealed: sent or given up it is removed (`removeOnComplete` and `removeOnFail`, proved in the issuer spec), the dead-letter copy keeps no data, and the lookup job holds only the address typed; sealing it like the invitation outbox, or sending the email inside the lookup job so that no job carries the token, closes the window: Step 7.3-B. (f) no global or depth cap before queueing on `auth-email`: the limiter of 30 a second also counts the `REQUEST_MAGIC_LINK` jobs (a database lookup that never reaches the provider), so a real link spends two slots, and the only brakes are 5 a minute per IP and per address, which a botnet with invented addresses passes; it saturates the 30 a second and delays real links (before this PR it did the same in the shared queue, so this is better but not closed): a global or queue-depth cap before queueing, with the alert of (c): owner Step 7.3-B or 7.4; (g) the two limiters are per worker process (N replicas allow N times 100 a second): a note for the capacity of 7.4; (h) the error of the provider may repeat the address in the dead-letter copy (`error.message`), accepted: the copy keeps the queue, the job name and the error and no job data. **Rollback runbook:** a rollback of the worker rolls the api back with it, and `auth-email` is emptied before the new worker returns (its jobs keep the address and the raw link in Redis until the 15 minutes of the link pass). (d) the `SEND_EMAIL` branch of `AuthEmailProcessor` repeats `EmailProcessor.sendEmail` (the ZodError mapping): one shared helper when the case of `EmailProcessor` for the magic link is removed in (a). **Review fixes:** the two email limiters now add up to the provider's 100 a second (70 for `email`, 30 for `auth-email`, `EmailProviderBudget`), the dead-letter copy of any `auth-email` job keeps no data (it held the address and the link), and the real worker module is proved to build `AuthEmailProcessor`.

The web takes the values from the `InvitationEmailStatus` constant, not literals. `aes-gcm` `decrypt` opens a format-1 payload even when `aad` is given (it has no data to check): that is the compatibility, and the comment says so. The view drops the sealed bytes and never carries the link. The web row says where the email stands; on `failed` it shows an alert and makes the existing Resend the main action (it is the same `POST .../resend`: same permissions, same per-address cooldown of 60 seconds counted from the invitation's creation, no bypass; a given-up email is about six hours old, so in practice it has passed; the alert says who must resend when the viewer cannot). The seal now binds `invitation-outbox:<storeId>:<invitationId>` as AES-GCM associated data: `aes-gcm` writes format 2 when given `aad` and format 1 otherwise, and opens both (format 2 never opens without its data, and a format-2 payload whose byte is lowered to 1 fails its tag), so a row sealed by the previous release (format 1, at most a few hours old) still opens and no migration is needed; the api chooses the invitation id before the insert to seal against it. **Decisions:** derive the status from the existing columns instead of storing it (no migration, nothing to keep in step); bind the seal instead of only documenting it (a sealed email copied to another row or store no longer opens, and the change is backward compatible); presence of the outbox is asked with a filtered second query (`emailOutbox: { not: null }`, ids only), so the sealed bytes are never read into the list path. **Rotation guide (HC-216), the invitation outbox:** before rotating `CREDENTIALS_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, wait until no invitation waits (`SELECT count(*) FROM invitations WHERE email_outbox IS NOT NULL` is 0; at most six hours after the last invite) or accept the loss: after the rotation a waiting row no longer opens, each delivery counts as a failed attempt, the row is given up after 12 attempts (about six hours) with its outbox cleared, and the inviter then sees `failed` in Settings > Team and resends (a new invitation, sealed with the new key). Nothing re-seals an outbox row, by design: the link is a secret that is cheaper to reissue than to migrate. **Deploy order:** the worker must run the new code before (or together with) the api: a worker of the previous release does not know format 2 and counts each open as a failed attempt (backoff 1, 2, 4 minutes...), so a rolling deploy that serves new seals to an old worker only delays the email until the new worker is up. **Proved (readers' request):** a format-2 email whose format byte is lowered to 1 does not open, with or without the associated data (the tag covers the data; `invitation-outbox.spec`, `credential-cipher.spec`), and a bound email never opens without its data. A replica of the previous release that receives format 2 fails closed: its open throws on the unknown version, the delivery counts one attempt, keeps the outbox and releases the claim, and the sweep retries after the backoff; once a reader that knows the format takes the row it is sent (`invitation-email-delivery.integration.spec`, with a version byte no release knows standing for the old reader; the old code itself is not run). The loss window is the twelve attempts (about six hours): a deploy that finishes inside it loses nothing. **Left (rule 12):** (g) the plain (format 1) fallback of `openInvitationEmail` ignores the associated data, so a legacy blob pasted on another row still opens: it only exists for rows sealed before this PR, which are given up within about six hours; remove the fallback (open with format 2 only) in the first release after it: Step 7.3-B; (h) an unreadable seal (key changed, data mismatch) is not terminal: it burns the 12 attempts (about six hours showing as on its way) before turning `failed`; counting a `DecryptionError` as terminal would tell the inviter at once: Step 7.3-B; (i) the web schema takes `emailStatus` as a strict enum, so web and api ship together; (e) the e2e of the `failed` row needs a way to age an invitation to given-up from the browser suite (today only the api integration spec writes the state directly): owner Step 7.7, with the other e2e of the invitation outbox; (f) the key rotation job (HC-216) does not exist yet, so the guide above is the whole procedure until it does: Step 7.3-B.

Proof: `tests/api/credentials-reseal.spec.ts` (as the worker role, RLS enforced, every column; foreign-key and damaged values left byte for byte; second run changes nothing; another organization untouched; no value in the audit or the log), unit specs for the mismatch, the conflict, the cap and the run without a previous key. **Decisions:** (a) a job of its own over every organization (rejected: riding on `RECONCILE_FINANCE`, which only visits organizations with books); (b) one target per COLUMN, so a failure or a cap is per column (rejected: per row, which would hide which secret failed); (c) plain `updateMany` with the old bytes in the WHERE (rejected: a DEFINER function per table, there is nothing to guard); (d) the readers switch to `openRotating` instead of making `open` fall back to the previous key (rejected: it would weaken the check "opens with the current key alone"). **Debt, all tracked:** (1) the FISCAL job still rides on the books, so the fiscal values of an organization without books are not visited (it holds none today); the runbook step 5 lists the organizations that hold a fiscal value so a difference blocks retiring the old key. Closes in Step 7.3 (a fiscal sweep over every organization, or `RESEAL_CREDENTIALS` also calling `FiscalResealer`), owner Step 7.3, condition: the query of the runbook returns the same ids as the log without relying on the books. (2) The swap bumps `updated_at` of the row (`@updatedAt`); nothing reads it for sync today. Closes in Step 7.3 if a reader of `updated_at` appears (pass the read value in `data`). (3) The CI of the rotation itself (an end-to-end run of the runbook with two real keys through api and worker) is the owner's rehearsal before the first rotation in production, listed in the runbook; owner: owner, condition: before step 2 of the runbook is run for real. (4) A value that never opens does not count against the cap of writes (fixed in this PR, as #933 did for the fiscal one); it counts against the cap of reads (`MAX_SCANNED_PER_TARGET`), so 50000 of them in one column would still stop the run. The operator has to resolve every failure before retiring the old key (runbook step 5). (5) The job is retried 3 times when any value fails, and each retry rescans the organization (one short transaction per value); the failure codes are deterministic, so a retry cannot help. Closes in Step 7.3: open the already-current check inside the page read, or do not retry a job whose failures are only `key_mismatch` / `row_damaged`. (7) The schema spec sees only `Bytes` columns: a sealed value kept as base64 in a text or JSON column, in Redis or in a job payload depends on the manual inventory above (OAuth session, DSR intake job); owner Step 7.3, closes with a spec that finds `.toString('base64')` next to `seal(` or by an explicit decision when one is added. (8) The error log of a run names at most `CredentialsReseal.MAX_LOGGED_FAILURES` (20) values; the rest are counted by code in the report. (9) The integration spec has one row per column in the usual state plus a legacy format-1 outbox, a second request and the other organization; a revoked plugin installation is not seeded (the target does not read the status). Closes in Step 7.3 if a status ever filters a target. (10) No spec kills the removal of the cap of reads (`MAX_SCANNED_PER_TARGET`, 50000): it would need more than 50000 rows; make the cap injectable if the service is touched again (owner Step 7.3). (11) `truncated` is only in the `info` log and the job does not fail for it; the runbook says explicitly that with `truncated: true` the previous key is NOT retired. A row that never opens fails the job every night and, with `removeOnFail`, only the log remains (declared in (5)); the runbook asks to keep those logs until the key is retired. (6) The count of the scheduler log is of jobs OFFERED to the queue (a same-day job id is deduplicated by BullMQ), not of new jobs.

The guards honour the setting only when the statement runs as the owner of that function (`fiscal_reseal_door_open`), so `platform_app` or `platform_worker` setting the name by hand still hit `immutable` (spec with both roles), and with the setting on it compares the whole row minus the two sealed columns (any other change, status included, is refused; spec). Runbook: `docs/CREDENTIALS_KEY_ROTATION_RUNBOOK.md` (the owner provides the new key and keeps the old one until two clean nights). **Decisions:** (a) the door is a function owner check, not the setting alone (rejected: the setting alone, forgeable by any role that can run `set_config`; a list of roles to exclude, closed by hand) ; (b) it runs inside the nightly books job per organization (rejected: a new queue and a cross-tenant list definer, more surface for the same result); (c) `key_mismatch` stays one code for a rotated key and an altered row (AES-GCM cannot tell them apart); (d) no attempt counter is persisted per value: each value is touched once per run and the cursor moves on, so a value that always fails cannot hold the queue; it is counted by code in the log and fails the job so the alarm of a failed job shows it. **Limits accepted:** (1) the SQL checks only the SHAPE of a new sealed value (version 1 or 2, at least 29 bytes), not that it opens to the same text: a compromised or buggy worker could leave a garbage receiver with a valid shape; the defence is the re-open of the service before the swap and the audit entry of each swap (owner: Step 7.3, close with a database-side check if the key ever lives there); (2) every row, current ones included, opens a short transaction only to decrypt: decrypt outside the unit and open the transaction only to write (before rotating a large organization, Step 7.3); (3) `truncated` is global to the run and sticky: safe, slower; (4) the owner role of the function passes the door by setting it by hand, as it could disable the trigger (runbook). the owner check does not protect an environment where the application connects AS that owner (a local dev superuser): there a raw statement could set the setting; production runs as `platform_app` and `platform_worker`. A run seals again at most `FiscalReseal.MAX_VALUES_PER_KIND` values per kind and night (the current ones do not count) and reports `truncated`; the runbook says not to retire the key while it is true. **Left, each with its owner and closing condition:** (i) Step 7.3-S11c, BEFORE the first rotation of the key in production: the sealed values outside the fiscal area (channel and carrier credentials, webhook secrets, OAuth sessions, plugin secrets, the closing-mail address) are not covered; the previous key does not serve them and the runbook says not to rotate until then; (ii) S11c: an organization without books has no night, so its fiscal data is not reached (a sweep over every organization, or run it from the issuer setup); (iii) Step 7.3: a gauge for `failed` and `resealed` of the run (today the log and the failed job are the signal); (iv) S11b-2 (this session): the masked receiver columns and their backfill, which will use the same door (the guard then compares the whole row minus the sealed and masked columns), the merge of customers that carries the fiscal data, and the nit of `openSealed` logging at error level on each failed attempt of a submit (once per document and window).
