- [ ] **The e2e suite and the rate limit of the api (2026-11-07, rule 12; measured for the coordinator; PR `test/e2e-spread-inbox-addresses`):** the api limits each ROUTE to 100 requests a minute for each address (a control the e2e exercises on purpose, #168, and that stays as it is). The 16 cases of `inbox.spec.ts` keep one session and so one address: measured with a logger of the requests of the api, `GET /conversations` was called 97 times on `main` (5ef53d8) and 94 on #212 (d56d822), 311 and 310 requests in all: the count did not grow, the suite sat at 94-97% of the limit of one route, and a slower run, a retry or one more list request tipped it into "Too many attempts" in cases that had nothing to do with it (the phone list, and the specs that ran in the same minute). Done: `reachServicesFromOwnAddress` returns a function that changes the address and `inbox.spec.ts` calls it before each case (the same session; the most any address then asks of one route in a minute is 15). **Left:** only `inbox.spec.ts` was measured; `customers.spec.ts`, `media-states.spec.ts`, `thread.spec.ts`, `templates.spec.ts` and `login.spec.ts` also keep a context for several cases and were not (the logger was a local patch and is not in the repository); `channels.spec:333` and `content-settings:131` failed with "Test timeout of 30000ms exceeded" and no "Too many attempts" in their snapshots, so their cause is still open. Known limits of the change: the address changes for the requests sent after the change (one still in flight from the case before counts against the new address), the realtime connection keeps its first address, the session of the inbox now moves between addresses from case to case (nothing in the product binds a session to an address today; the grace path of the refresh only logs `ipChanged`: if that changes, these cases will say so), and nothing asserts the count of a case stays small.
- [ ] **The chat UX list of the owner, W2: the page that scrolls (2026-11-07, rule 12; evidence `chat-ux-repro.md` and a capture of the owner; PR `fix/thread-layout-scroll`):** with no conversation open the page was still; opening one made it scroll as a whole (the header went out of sight and a white gap stayed under the thread, with a picture of a thumb with no height limit). Cause found (measured by the QA in a real Chrome, which replaced the first guess): the hidden texts of the sent replies (`sr-only`, which is `position: absolute`) had a container OUTSIDE the scroller of the thread (the scroller was not `relative`), so they escaped its clip and made the height of the whole page grow, and the wheel at the end of the thread went on to scroll the page; `relative` and `overscroll-contain` on the scrollers of the thread, the list, the sidebar, the notification panel, the customer drawer and the gallery fix it. Other causes found on the way: the inbox was `-m-4 h-[calc(100dvh-3.5rem)]` inside a frame with `min-h-dvh`, a height computed from the size of the top bar that was a few pixels off (1 to 22 measured), and `scrollIntoView` (jump to a quoted message) moves every scrollable ancestor, the page included. Done: on the routes of the inbox (`isInboxPath`, read from the address so it is right in the first draw and in every browser) the frame of the app is exactly the window, with `overflow-clip` (a browser cannot scroll it to reveal a focused field) and no padding; the top bar takes what it needs and the inbox the rest, so the panes scroll on their own; the top bar (brand, store, links, bell, account) no longer overflows at 485 or 390 px, which the clipped inbox would have made unreachable and which also fixes the page of customers: the brand and the store name shorten, the links scroll on their own, and the bell and the account menu never leave the window (the e2e measures the boxes of the store and account buttons at 1280, 485 and 390 px, and that /customers has no sideways scroll at 485); the jump to a message moves only the thread (centred, or by its top when the message is taller than the thread); an e2e (`inbox.spec.ts`, with 14 sent replies and the wheel to the end and past it) checks at 1536, 1280, 485 and 390 px that the page is as tall as the window, stays at the top, and that the top bar and the box to write in are inside the window. On a phone the filters and the list of conversations are one column that scrolls as a whole and the list has a height of its own (`70dvh`): with the frame fixed, the filters alone are taller than a phone window and left the list with no height (found by the e2e of the phone in CI). The e2e opens the conversation once and resizes the window under it (the api limits a person to 100 requests a minute per address, and a first version with five page loads made the following specs of the run fail with "Too many attempts": `channels.spec:333`, `content-settings:131`, `invitations:74`, the phone list, which looked like flaky tests and were this). **Left:** not run in a browser by the author (the e2e of CI is the check); the thumb with no height limit of the capture was not reproduced (the pictures of the thread already have fixed boxes), so nothing was added for it; the jump to a quoted message has no e2e; the mobile keyboard (`dvh` does not shrink with it) was not tested.

The route of the revisions of a deleted message gives the list (without text) only to who holds `MESSAGES_VIEW_DELETED` and an empty list to anyone else, so the edits do not leak who edited and when. **Left:** the row keeps its edit fields (`pendingContent`, `editStatus`) for the worker: a customer message that arrives deleted by a channel tombstone while an edit is in flight is not covered by the lock that blocks deleting a queued edit, and the api view reports no edit then; the list preview of a deleted message already carried no text.
- [ ] **The chat UX list of the owner, W3c: new messages and the day that floats (2026-11-07, rule 12; PR `feat/new-messages-pill-sticky-date`):** done: when messages arrive while the reader is above the end of the thread, a button "N new messages" (`unseenAfter`, tested) takes them to the end; the conversation is marked read only when the reader is at the end (`useMarkRead(…, isReading)`), where before it was marked as soon as a message arrived whatever the reader was looking at; while the reader scrolls, the day of the top of the view floats over the thread (`stickyDayOf`, tested, found once for each frame) and goes away 1.5 s after the last scroll (it is `aria-hidden`: the separators of the days are in the list already); an e2e (`thread-reading.spec.ts`) covers the floating day. An e2e (`widget.spec.ts`) covers the button: a visitor writes through the widget while the agent reads above the end, the button "1 new message" appears, the conversation stays unread until the button is pressed and is read then, and a reply of the agent shows no button. **Left:** only the messages of the customer count as new (what the agent wrote, from this tab or another, and the system lines do not); nothing floats while the reader is at the end (so not on opening or when a message makes the thread follow itself); the end is worked out again when the thread or its window changes size, not only on a scroll; a mark that ends well looks again for a message that arrived while it was in flight; the button respects reduced motion, is said to a screen reader through a polite region and hands the focus to the last message; there is no test of `useMarkRead` (no DOM environment), the manual QA covers that nothing is marked read while the reader is above the end.
- [x] **The e2e cases that timed out at 30 s, `channels.spec:333` and `content-settings:131` (2026-11-07, rule 12; measured from the traces of the failed runs of #219 and #222; PR `test/e2e-signin-waits-outside-timeout`):** the traces of both cases show NO action of the browser between the creation of the page and the timeout: the case was inside `waitForLinkBudget`, the wait that keeps the specs under `MagicLinkThrottle` (5 links a minute for each address, and the specs share `admin@test.com`). - [x] **The chat UX list of the owner, W3d: one state machine for the files of the thread (2026-11-07, rule 12; PR `feat/media-single-skeleton`):** the worker stores a customer's message first and fetches its file after, so the thread drew the word of the kind ("Image", with an icon) for that moment and then the skeleton: two different looks before the picture. Tests: `media-state.spec.ts` and two cases in `media-states.spec.ts` (the box of a file not stored yet, and the box kept while the links are slow). **Decisions and limits:** the skeleton waits at most `MediaArrival.WINDOW_MS` (10 minutes) after the message; after it a message with no file reads as the word again, so a file that is gone does not pulse for ever (the clock is read once, when the message is first drawn, so a thread left open does not flip it). Limits accepted: the first toast of a session shows after the chunk arrives and a moment (100 ms) for the live region to exist, so a screen reader announces it; the wrapper offers `toast`, `success`, `error`, `info` and `warning` with their options and no id, `dismiss`, `loading` or `promise` (nothing uses them; widen the bridge when something does); the host and the Toaster have no component test because the web project has no DOM environment (the queue is tested, and the e2e specs that read toasts cover the whole path); a load of sonner that fails is retried by the next toast and never takes the page down; the queue keeps the newest 20. Limits: log only (not in the run summary), taken from the run that is the median of the scripts, silent (an empty listing) when the audit is missing from the report, and the format of the lines was not checked against a real run when it was written. Each button is a plain one, with the attributes Radix gives a closed trigger, until the person points at it, focuses it or presses it; then its code is downloaded (`OnDemandMenu`, `components/shared/on-demand-menu.tsx`: a `lazy` module and a `Suspense` whose fallback is the same button) and the press that asked for it opens it as soon as it is here (`defaultOpen`), so the first press is not lost and Radix moves the focus in and gives it back. Messenger, Instagram and the widget are unchanged (one text, under the first file; the Meta plugin sends it as a second message). **Decisions:** a column over an inference from the channel (the view in core cannot know the plugin, and an old message must keep reading as before); the text goes last only when every file went (a text that overtakes a failed file would reach the customer first) and it is not retried by itself (Meta has no key for it: `unconfirmed`, the agent resends it). **Debts:** (a) the real test with Meta of the field of the first file and of the text last (Step 7.3, line of the Meta findings); (b) a message queued BEFORE this deploy and still unsent is sent as before (text under its first file), by design; (c) editing the `content` of a message with `textApart` would target the id of the first file: WhatsApp takes no edits, so nothing offers it, and a channel that takes edits and declares `CAPTION_PER_FILE` must bind `editMessage` to `captionChannelMessageId` (Step 5.6, contract of `CAPTION_PER_FILE`); (d) `resend-caption` of a text apart does not check that the files after the first were delivered (it checks the message did not fail), same as before (Step 7.3). (e) Found by `/code-review`, same gap as the text of a WhatsApp audio sent apart: deleting the message deletes only the id of the first file, not `captionChannelMessageId`, and the receipts (delivered, read, failed) match `channelMessageId` and `media.channelMessageId` only, so a late failure of the text apart is dropped (Step 7.3: delete the second id too, and match receipts on `captionChannelMessageId`); (f) a text held back because a file failed has no state of its own (`captionState` stays null until the files are resent), and a failed write of the `unconfirmed` mark leaves the text unsent with null state: the agent sees the failed file or, in the second case, only the log (Step 7.3: a `pending` caption state). **Fixed in this PR:** the retention purge also clears `media.caption`, and the conversation export writes the text under each file after the text of the message.

- [ ] **Validate the NOT VALID constraints in the maintenance window before the first deployment (owner 7.5; PR 7.3-S5):** with the owner's credential (`DIRECT_DATABASE_URL`, never in the repository), `pnpm db:constraints:validate status`, then `pnpm db:constraints:validate run --confirm=<database>`, then `status` again must say `17 of 17 constraints are valid`; if one is `violated`, follow `docs/NOT_VALID_CONSTRAINTS_RUNBOOK.md`. Closed when the run is written in the deployment log.
- [ ] **Fit the per-person quota in staging (owner's decision, 2026-11-21; metrics from PR `feat/http-user-rate-limit-metrics`):** the quota of 600 a minute per person (`AuthenticatedUserRateLimit`, Step 7.1-B) stays as it is. Done when staging has run with real use and the dashboard reads `platform_rate_limit_budget_usage_ratio{throttler="user:authenticated"}` and the rate of `platform_rate_limit_hits_total`: if the p99 of a person's requests a minute goes past ~300 (the ratio is weighted by requests, not by person: read it as the share of observations above `le="0.5"`, `1 - rate(platform_rate_limit_budget_usage_ratio_bucket{le="0.5"}[5m]) / rate(platform_rate_limit_budget_usage_ratio_count[5m])`, over 1 %, and look in the logs at who makes them before raising anything for everybody: one bot or one export is not broad pressure) or there is any sustained 429, either the quota goes up or the reads and the realtime traffic get a bucket of their own, apart from the writes (decide with the numbers, in a PR with a real change). The ratio is weighted by requests, so the highest bucket reached says how close the busiest person came.

Debts, kept on purpose: (a) the command reports the encryption but does not apply it, and does not create the bucket, the replica or the IAM roles (provider tooling, owner only, runbook prerequisites 1, 4, 5); (b) MFA delete is not supported by the command (the runbook says what to do); (c) a rehearsal against a real S3-compatible provider is the owner's, the specs prove the logic and not a provider's behavior (runbook prerequisite 6), closed by the next bullet. (d) `apply` turns versioning on before it writes the rule, so a sweep run that starts in those seconds can rewrite an original before the 30-day rule exists (no data is lost, the rule covers versions by age): the runbook tells the operator to apply in a quiet window with the worker stopped or between two sweep runs; the next bullet (the owner's act) carries that condition. Requests of the command have a 10 s connection and 30 s request timeout; `scripts/lib/bucket-protection-entry.spec.ts` runs the entry point (environment, local refusals, no credential printed, exit codes) without network.

- [x] **Two identical webhooks at once (OPS-SET-460, fix PR, rule 12):** `POST /settings/webhooks` twice at once made two webhooks, and each event was delivered twice. Migration `20270118100000_webhooks_unique_target` (rollback idempotent) adds the partial unique index `uq_webhooks_store_url_events` on `(store_id, url, events) WHERE status <> 'disabled'`; the schema sorts the events (the same set is the same array) and the migration sorts the existing rows and **disables, not deletes,** the later copies of a pair that already exists (they keep their secret and their log). The service answers `RESOURCE_CONFLICT` to a create or an update that loses to the index, so two requests at once give one 201 and the rest 409, and turning a disabled copy on beside the active one is a 409 too. The address is stored as the URL standard writes it (`new URL(url).href`), so two spellings of one address are one; rows made before keep their spelling (no SQL can rewrite them safely). The conflict carries `metadata.reason = duplicate_webhook` (`WebhookConflictReasons`). The index holds `md5(url)`, not the url (a long address would not fit a btree entry). Rejected: unique `(store_id, url)` (a store may follow different events at one address) and deleting the old copies (loses a secret a receiver may be using). **Debt (Step 7.4, web):** the webhook dialog shows the generic text of `RESOURCE_CONFLICT`; give the duplicate its own i18n text en/es from `metadata.reason`; the copies the migration disabled still count toward `WebhookLimits.MAX_PER_STORE` and the store is not told (the owner is the only store in the MVP: Phase 2 decides whether disabled ones leave the count).

- [x] **From Step 5.6 (Left by PR C4, rule 12), closed in PR 7.3-S3 (`fix/plugin-api-limit-before-key-lookup`):** the per-address limit on the failures of a plugin key. The flood guard of the address (`PluginApiIpThrottle`, 3000 a minute, the global throttler) already ran before `PluginApiKeyGuard` but counts every call and is far too high to bound a probe, and it runs after the body parser. Now `PluginKeyProbeLimiter` (`libs/core/http`, counter `plugin_key_probe`, `PluginApiKeyProbeThrottle`: 30 failures a minute per address, blocked for the window) is asked first thing in the guard, before the key is hashed and looked up, and by `pluginEventsBodyParser` before a byte of the 1 MiB body is read (an address that has to wait gets Nest's 100 KB parser and then 429); only the failures of a key that is missing, malformed or unknown are counted (a key that exists but is revoked, disabled or of a suspended plugin is no guess and is not counted, so one rotated installation that keeps retrying cannot lock out its healthy siblings behind the same address), so a plugin with a good key is not slowed by its own traffic (but see debt (a): an address that is over the limit is refused whatever key it carries). An address that has to wait is answered 429 with `Retry-After` by the parser too (never a 413 for a good batch), and the large reads in flight of one address are capped per replica (`RemoteChannelApiLimits.EVENTS_CONCURRENT_READS_PER_ADDRESS`, 8) because the failures are counted after the lookup and a burst that arrives together would all read first. Every failed key answers the same 401 and takes at least `PluginApiKeyRefusalFloorMs` (100 ms), so the clock does not say how far the lookup went. The refusals are counted in `rate_limit_hits_total{throttler="plugin_key_probe"}` (no address label). **Decisions (rule 12):** (1) failures only, counted with the block of `RedisThrottlerStorage` and read without counting (`blockedFor`), rejected: counting every call (it would hold a plugin by its own traffic) and a per-address limit on the lookup alone (the body is read before the guard). (2) Redis down lets the call through (as the other limits of the address do): a key has 256 bits and the limit of the installation still fails closed. (3) A sleep floor and not a constant-time lookup: the lookups are several queries of different cost and the floor is the smaller change. **Debts:** (a) an attacker who shares the egress address of a real plugin can block that plugin for a minute with 30 made-up keys (a wrong `TRUST_PROXY_HOPS` makes every caller one address: the limiter keeps no counter for a call with no address, but a proxy address that is wrong is still one); the owner can raise `PluginApiKeyProbeThrottle.limit` or key it by address and key prefix: Step 7.4 if it shows in the metric; (b) the `Retry-After` of the 429 is the remaining block, the same for every refusal of the window: no debt, noted; (e) the key of the limit is the whole address, so an attacker who rotates the IPv6 addresses of one /64 evades it; grouping IPv6 by /64 is Step 7.4 if the metric shows it; (d) the case `refuses a body past 1 MiB with 413` of `plugin-events-body-parser.spec.ts` fails here with `write EPIPE` on the maintainer's Mac (also on a clean `main`) and passes in the CI of `main` (the `unit-tests` job of the runs of #884 and #883): it is the local environment (the server closes the socket while the client still writes 1 MiB), not the code; a fix of the spec that reads the 413 before the client finishes writing is Step 7.7; (c) `tests/api` has no end-to-end case of the 31st failed key (it needs Docker): the unit specs of the guard, the limiter and the parser cover it, and `redis-throttler.storage.integration.spec.ts` covers `blockedFor`: Step 7.7.

CONCURRENTLY`, `DETACH PARTITION ... CONCURRENTLY` and a schema-qualified name are not detected (a file with `INDEX CONCURRENTLY` that does not fit fails, the safe side); `customers.search_vector` and `products.search_vector` stay: owner Step 7.3, condition of closing: check the same way that no read uses them, then drop them in their own PR; (e) the migrations that create the search indexes take a write lock on `messages` and `customers` while they build (Prisma runs a migration in a transaction): a deploy on a large table needs a maintenance window; (from Step 5.2 PR C3) a per-user rate limit on `POST /search/clicks`

- [ ] **Response headers of the bucket (QA fix PR Q6, SEC-3414):** the files the api signs are served by the bucket, not by the api, and S3 lets a signed URL set the type and the disposition only (`ResponseContentType` and `ResponseContentDisposition`, which the api fixes from the row: an uploaded file is always an attachment and the type is the one the bytes were checked against). It cannot set `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` or a `Content-Security-Policy: sandbox`. Put a response-headers policy (CloudFront, or the bucket's own) in front of the production bucket that adds `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` and `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; sandbox` to every object, and check it with `curl -I` on a signed URL. The development bucket (SeaweedFS) does not add them; the check of the first bytes at the confirmation (`matchesDeclaredType`) is what keeps a page out of the bucket there.

A deploy with the wrong `CREDENTIALS_ENCRYPTION_KEY` therefore flips and notifies every store at once. Decide here whether the api and the worker check at start-up that a sample connection opens and refuse to boot otherwise, and put it in the deployment checklist next to the key rotation. Also: an outbound send with unreadable credentials is retried like any failure and its last attempt fails the message with `CHANNEL_CREDENTIALS_INVALID` (a worker with another key for a while loses nothing), and it does not touch the connection; the health round is what marks it, so the state follows within one round

- [ ] **Hardening of the media pipeline found by the review of the media PR, in code that PR did not change (rule 12):** (a) `HEAVY_PROCESSING` has `attempts: 2` with a 5 s backoff (`queue-job-options.ts`), so a scanner outage of about ten seconds makes the last attempt of `scan` run `giveUp`, which marks the file `UNSCANNABLE` and deletes it from the bucket; a customer file the provider will not hand over again is lost. Give the scan more attempts with a backoff of minutes, or give up by age of the row. **(a) closed by PR 7f-B1 (2026-11-24):** every `SCAN_FILE` job is added with `scanFileJobOptions` (8 tries, exponential from 5 s, about ten minutes in all; the other jobs of the heavy queue keep their two), and `giveUp` keeps a row `pending` with its file until the scanner has been failing for `UploadLimits.SCAN_GIVE_UP_HOURS` (6 h; counted from the first job that ended with no verdict, so a row that is old because its first job was lost is not given up by the first outage it meets): nothing is served or sent meanwhile (only `clean` is), and the sweep of stuck scans queues it again; only past that age is the row `unscannable` and the file deleted. **Left on purpose by that PR (owner: Step 7.3):** (i) the sweep of stuck scans runs with the hourly cleanup (`:50`) and takes rows older than `STUCK_SCAN_MINUTES` (30), so an outbound video or audio file whose tool stays away more than the ten minutes of the job waits up to ~80 min after the tool is back (QA MED-043/131 measured at +34 min, before the first pass that could take them; they were `pending`, the sweep was never broken); give the stuck-scan pass a schedule of its own (every 10 min, own lock) if that wait matters; (ii) a file that waits for the scanner for hours shows the 409 `FILE_NOT_READY` of a pending file, with no text that says the scanner is down; (iii) a file that clamd answers with an `ERROR` of its own (size limit, a crafted file) is tried like an outage: 8 tries per generation and one generation per sweep for the 6 hours, then given up as before; separate "clamd answered about this file" from "clamd is not there" and keep the short retry for the first kind (not done here: an `ERROR` can also be transient, and deleting on it risks a customer file); (iv) a long outage re-queues every pending file once an hour, each with 8 tries, so the dead-letter queue and the error log fill about six times per file: skip the re-queue while the scanner is known to be down, or log and dead-letter only the final give-up; (v) the failed-job branch of the sweep (a finished job keeps its id and is removed before the new one is added) is pre-existing code and has no spec of its own: a worker started inside jest left connections open and hung the suite, so it was checked once by hand against BullMQ (a job failed by a worker, removed, added again: waiting); give it a spec with a queue-level fake. (b) A store image is decoded three times (once per variant) with the 100 million pixel ceiling, against 25 million for an avatar, and the heavy queue runs two jobs at once: decode once to the big variant and derive the other two from it, lower `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`, and set sharp's processing timeout. (c) Every sharp error is final (`UnrecoverableError` for a message image; for an avatar `UNSCANNABLE` and the file deleted), including a resource error such as running out of memory, which the queue should retry; and a message image is decoded with sharp's default `failOn` while the avatar uses `failOn: 'error'`, so a photo with a flaw in its tail is refused. (d) `processAvatar`, unlike `processImage` (fixed in the media PR: guarded `updateMany` and the variant keys deleted when the row is gone), still writes with no guard on a row that may have been removed. (e) `processAvatar` deletes its deterministic final key when its update matches no row, even if a second run already finished and the row points at it: delete only when the row is gone. (f) In `media.service.ts` the confirmation drops the staging object and the requester key for any error of the signature check, including a transient bucket failure, and `dropStaging` logs the raw error and the key: clean up only for a refusal, and log `errorName`. (g) Tests: the pixel limit is tested only for avatars (add a store image), the give-up case does not assert that `MEDIA_UNSCANNABLE` is announced, `signVariant` has no case for a key outside the store prefix, and `tests/api/media.spec.ts` writes `3_600_000` and status codes as literals (`QUOTA_WINDOW_MS`, `HttpStatusCodes`). **Partly done (PR `chore/media-mailbox-config`, 2026-11-22):** the literals of `tests/api/media.spec.ts` are `QUOTA_WINDOW_MS` and `HttpStatusCodes`, and `signVariant` has its cases (a key of another store, no variant, a value that is not JSON of variants; `media-sign-variant.spec.ts`). **Still open (g):** the pixel limit of a store image, the assertion that the give-up case announces `MEDIA_UNSCANNABLE`. Owner: Step 7.3.

Now: `EmailDeliveryError` (`libs/core/email`) holds the name and the code of what the provider refused (plain tokens only, no `cause`, no provider text); `EmailService.send` turns any other error of the provider into one and lets a `ZodError` of the template through; `ResendProvider` throws it with the name and the status; for the queues `auth-email` and `email` and for the jobs `SEND_EMAIL` and `REQUEST_MAGIC_LINK` on any queue, `failedAttempt` logs `errorName` only (not `err`) and the dead-letter `error` is the name, or the fixed text of a `JobRejectedError`, `EmailDeliveryError` or `MailJobFailedError`; the queues are decided by `MAIL_QUEUES` and the job names by `REDACTED_JOBS` (one place; a new job that carries an address on another queue must be added to `REDACTED_JOBS`). The errors that a mail job can throw are all safe now (`EmailDeliveryError` from the provider, `MailJobFailedError` from the lookup of the address in `issueMagicLinkSafely`, which both processors of the magic link use, and the fixed text of `JobRejectedError`), so the `failedReason` and the stack that BullMQ keeps are safe too. Tests: `processor-support.spec` with the real pino and `REDACTED_PATHS` and SMTP-like and Resend-like errors, `email.service.spec`, `resend.provider.spec`, the dead letter of the integration spec; each dies under mutation. **Decision:** fix at the source (the service and the provider) and again in `failedAttempt` (so a raw error from any other code of a mail job is also kept out); rejected: a text scrubber for addresses in the redaction of the log (it would guess at free text and not cover the dead letter or `failedReason`). **Debts:** (a) the lookup of the address by `MagicLinkIssuer.issue` is wrapped (a reader found that a database error names the row it could not write); an error thrown by any other code that a mail job calls (the notice ledger, the delivery of an invitation) is not wrapped, because those services log the name only and their errors hold ids, not addresses: owner Step 7.3, to be checked again when a new job of mail is added; (b) the other queues log `err` as before: none of them holds an address by design, but a review of the errors that a channel plugin or a carrier raises with a phone number in them belongs to the S13 redaction item above.

The tenant cache expires on its own (`CacheTTL.VERY_SHORT`), so a deleted or renamed store can still be resolved by the guards for that time when Redis is down; nothing retries the invalidation. (e) The original of an image keeps its EXIF and GPS data (only the variants are re-encoded): decide with the owner whether the original is served at all or stripped on upload, a privacy decision; until then the download of an image is the original. ### Step 7.8 — Connect with Facebook (OAuth) for Messenger and Instagram
Owner decision (2026-11-05, nine questions answered yes): the provider's own login in place of a token pasted by hand, as the next feature after the three channels were connected. The design is in the owner's QA folder (`meta-oauth-diseno.md`); what it settled, and what was measured on 2026-11-06 in the Graph API Explorer with the owner's account (app `omnichannel-dev`, no secret or token left in any chat): classic Facebook Login with `response_type=code` (the token never passes through the browser), no `config_id` (Facebook Login for Business with a system-user token is what gave a token with no assets); `me/accounts` answers nothing for a Page that belongs to a portfolio, `me/businesses` (two portfolios) and `owned_pages` find it and carry its `access_token`, and the token of that Page reads the linked Instagram account with no error 100/33; reading a Page by its id needs `pages_read_engagement`, and the dialog lets the person clear it. The credential does not change: the login ends in the same `{ accessToken }` of the Page and in the same `connect`, so the account-in-use check, reconnection, audit, subscription and encryption are reused. The core owns the `state`, the exchange and the session; a plugin only answers about its provider (`ChannelPlugin.oauth`). WhatsApp stays out (Embedded Signup is Phase 2); a pasted token always stays as a link ("Use a manual token") and the two kinds of connection live together; disconnecting does not revoke at Meta; business verification and App Review wait until the platform opens to other people (Phase 2).

### Step 7.9 — Channel-agnostic core (owner's mandate, 2026-11-09; before Milestone 4)

Core, SDK, web and api-client must not know a channel by name: everything is decided by data the plugin declares
(its descriptor), so that a third party adds a channel without editing core or UI. Only `libs/channels/*` knows
its provider. The audit and the PR order are in the owner's reports (`auditoria-agnostico.md`, 28 findings); the
database has no CHECK or enum that blocks a new plugin id (verified), so no migration is planned.

## Dependency graph

```
M0 Foundation
 └─> M1 Auth and tenancy
      ├─> M2 Core messaging
      │    └─> M3 Inbox interface
      │         └─> M4 Commerce
      │              └─> M5 Operations
      │                   ├─> M6 Monetization (DEFERRED, Phase 2)
      │                   └─> M7 Production readiness
      │                        └─> M8 Enhancements (only 8.3 in MVP)
      └─> (inside M1, Step 1.0 Queues and email runs first: the magic link of 1.1 needs it)
```

**Critical path:** 0.3 constants → 0.4 schema → 1.2 tenancy → 2.6 inbound
pipeline → 3.2 inbox. Everything else can be parallelized around it.

---

## Rules for the executor

1. **Never skip Step 0.3.** Constants are a blocking dependency.
2. **Every new tenant-scoped resource** gets added to the tenant isolation
   suite in the same PR that introduces it (`check-isolation-coverage` enforces it).
3. **Every migration ships with a rollback script** (`check-rollbacks` enforces it).
4. **Every endpoint** has `AuthGuard`, `TenantGuard` and a permission decorator unless it is
   explicitly public (`ApiRoutes.webhooks.*`, `ApiRoutes.widget.*`, invitation preview and
   accept, auth magic-link endpoints, DSR verify, health). `AccessLevelGuard` joins this list in Phase 2.
5. **`storeId` comes from `X-Store-Id` through `TenantGuard`** — never from a body or query.
6. **No user-facing string is hardcoded.** i18n keys only — including persisted notifications.
7. **The pre-push hook (`pnpm validate:affected`) must pass** before any push, `pnpm validate:ci` before any PR, and `pnpm validate:all` is the full local run; the hooks never replace CI.
8. **When the TDD is ambiguous, stop and ask.** Do not invent a design.
9. **Anything marked MATURE or Phase 2 is out of scope** unless this plan
   explicitly includes it.
10. **A step is done only when its PR is green on GitHub** with every CI job that exists at
    that point. When a step creates a CI job, it also says which check to add to the `main`
    ruleset (see "CI rollout"); add it after the job has run once.

## Progress tracking

One row per step. The checkboxes inside each step track its tasks; this table tracks the step itself, with the
pull request that delivered it. **The step's own PR updates its row**, so the progress lives in the repository and
moves with the code.

| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `todo` | not started |
| `in progress` | a branch for the step exists and is not merged |
| `done` | merged to `main` with every task checked and the "Done when" criterion verified |
| `deferred (Phase 2)` | out of the v1.2 MVP, kept for later |

How to keep it:
1. When the work on a step starts, the first commit of its branch sets the row to `in progress`.
2. When the step is complete, the last commit of its PR sets `done`, checks the step's task boxes, and fills in the PR
   number and the date (open the PR first to know its number, then add it as the last commit).
3. One step, one branch, one independent PR from an up-to-date `main`; never stack PRs.
   Never open a PR that only changes documentation: the row, the boxes and any doc fix travel inside the step's own PR,
   or inside the next PR that carries a real change.
4. Step 2.1 does not exist: it moved to Step 1.0. Step 8.3 is optional and is not needed to complete the MVP.

The MVP is complete when every row that is not `deferred` and not optional is `done`: **49 steps**.

Findings that no QA fix PR takes, with the step that closes each:

- [ ] **SEC-2 (conditional P2):** accepting an invitation spends the quota and blocks the IP for an hour (3 per hour) on any attempt. Rises to P2 if the proxy is badly configured. Step 7.5 (deployment: trusted proxy, then decide the limit) (task in Step 7.5)
- [ ] **`/metrics` is public** (declared in the report as known). Step 7.5 (task already in Step 7.5: "`/metrics` and the probes share the port of the service")
- [ ] **Sweeps can starve behind rows that always fail (review of Q1):** `SnoozeWakeScheduler` and `AutoArchiveScheduler` take the oldest due rows first and only log a failed one, so 200 or more rows that fail for good would hide the healthy ones behind them. Nothing makes a row fail for good today (a refused change is a person who got there first, and the next query no longer finds it); Step 7.6 adds an alert on the warn line of these two jobs and, if it ever fires, a retry counter or a skip list (task in Step 7.6)
- [ ] **The `security-tests` job runs out of heap as specs are added (found in Q2, PR #165):** `pnpm test:security` ran every spec of `tests/` in one Jest process (`--runInBand`, heap 4096 MB) and the heap grows with each spec file (every spec builds its own Nest app); at 48 passing files the 50th, the new notifications spec, crashed it twice in CI with `JavaScript heap out of memory` (no assertion failed; `main` passed with 49 files). Q2 splits the run into two shards (`--shard=1/2` and `2/2`, each its own process; since PR 375 each in its own CI job, and `security-tests` fails if either does): that is margin, not a cure, because the heap per spec file still grows. Step 7.3 (CI of the hardening pass) finds why a spec keeps its app in memory after `afterAll` (a leak in a shared helper or a service that is never closed) and, if it cannot be fixed, adds a shard when a shard passes 40 files (task in Step 7.3). **Found again in PR #529:** at the start of `products-search-performance.spec.ts`, the last of shard 4/4, the heap was 3.6 of the 4 GB and the major collections (330, 510, 948 ms, measured with a GC observer over the whole shard run locally) failed the 200 ms p95 of the search; the server-side time in CI was healthy (p95 at most 77 ms). The spec now runs in a process of its own (`tests/jest.latency.config.cts`, `pnpm test:latency`, a step of what was shard 4/4 and is now the last shard) and the security config ignores it. The leak that fills the heap is still open and belongs to Step 7.3 (this task); when it is closed the latency spec can return to the shards, or stay apart. **Shards raised to five (PR `fix/ci-security-shards-five`):** with about 35 spec files per shard at four, shards 1/4 and 2/4 of PR #542 hit the heap limit; the fix is one shard more (`1/5` to `5/5`, the denominator is in `ci.yml` and in `tests/project.json`), not a higher memory limit, which only moves the wall. The shard count lives in two places that must agree (the matrix of `ci.yml` and the `for` of `tests/project.json`); Step 7.3 may derive one from the other with a validator. Step 7.3 watches the files per shard (the `peak memory used on the runner` line of each shard) and moves to seven when a shard passes 29 files (the count at six, 174 files; one more spec lifts a shard to 30), which is the only trigger: the old 3 GB trigger of the runner peak is retired, because the peak was 6514 MB at the crash and no figure under it warned **Six shards (PR `ci/security-shards-6`, after the run of #588):** shard 4/5 of the run 43969526825 died with `JavaScript heap out of memory` (4055 MB of 4096 at the last mark-compacts, runner peak 6514 MB) with 35 spec files in the process; six shards put 29 in each (`1/6` to `6/6`, in `ci.yml` and `tests/project.json`; the latency step still runs in the last shard through `strategy.job-total`; the required checks of the `main` ruleset do not change, only the aggregator `security-tests`). The heap was not raised and no spec was skipped. **Left open for this task (Step 7.3), each with its owner here:** (a) the specs that grow the memory the most are not known: measure `--logHeapUsage` per spec of a shard and list the heaviest (each builds a Nest app, and the ones that also start a worker, a plugin server or a socket gateway keep more); (b) the split by file count does not weigh a spec, so one shard can get the heavy ones; a sequencer that weighs by measured heap needs recorded figures that drift, so the first step is (a); (c) a spec-leak check: a test that runs a spec twice in one process and fails when the heap after the second `afterAll` is above the first by more than a margin, which finds the app that is never closed; (d) the shard count lives in two places (the matrix of `ci.yml` and the `for` of `tests/project.json`) and a validator should read one from the other (**closed by PR 7.3-B2:** `pnpm validate:ci-shards`; the latency and plan specs left the last shard for their own job, `security-isolated-specs`); (e) the trigger for seven shards is the one above; the cut from 35 to 29 files per process is 17%, a thin margin, so (a) to (c) come before the next shard is paid for, and each extra shard repeats the setup (three services, install, migrate) on every PR run.

Its switch stays hidden (`NotificationTypesWithoutEmitter`); the step that first handles an order payment raises it and removes it from the list. No step of the plan charges an order: Steps 6.2 (Stripe) and 6.4 (Dunning) bill the platform's own subscriptions, not a store's orders, and Steps 4.3 and 4.9 do not. Step 4.3 decides it when it closes: the owner confirms that orders are cash on delivery only in v1.2 (then this line moves to Phase 2 with no step) or adds a step for card payments of orders next to 6.2 (task in Step 4.3)

The type, its text and its default stay in the matrix for the plugin runtime of Phase 2; QA fix PR Q7 decided: the preferences page hides the switch of a type nothing raises (`NotificationTypesWithoutEmitter`), `plugin.error` among them, until the plugin runtime of Phase 2 (Step 5.6 for the integration plugins that run) raises it and removes it from that list; the type, its text and its default stay (task already in Step 5.6: "Show the notification switch of this step")

Nothing is saved until the person saves, and the zone is a select they can change. Step 7.1 (give `GET /settings/business-hours` the zone of the store when the hours are empty) (task in Step 7.1)

The reply is the saved reply as stored (no variables are filled in), it is not translated, and a store whose channel window is closed at that moment sends nothing. - [x] **Shared pinned request and delivery helpers, atomic cap of webhooks a day (Step 7.3-B5, PR `refactor/plugin-shared-helpers`; closes debt (d) and (h) of PR P3, (a) of PLG-256, (a) of 5.4 and (b) of W1; rule 12).** (1) `libs/core/url-safety/src/pinned-request.ts` (`openPinnedRequest`) is the one recipe of a request to an address from outside (https, the checked addresses only through `pinnedLookup`, a socket of its own, the certificate against the name); `pinnedHttpsExchange`, `pinnedHttpsGet` and `createPinnedFetch` use it, and the worker's `pinnedHttpsPost` is now `pinnedHttpsExchange` with the new `discardBody` option (the answer is never read), mapping its failures to `WebhookPostFailed` with the same `retryable` rule (its spec is unchanged). (2) `WebhookDeliveryRecorder` (`apps/worker/src/webhooks/webhook-delivery-recorder.ts`) writes a delivery down for both kinds (metric, log row, count of failures in a row, the twentieth-failure turn-off told once, the parent deleted while the delivery ran); each deliverer gives it a `DeliveryBinding` with its own columns. (3) `PluginWebhookDayCap` (`plugin-webhook-day-cap.ts`): the cap of `limits.maxWebhooksPerDay` is one atomic Lua step in Redis over a sorted set of delivery ids scored by their start (`CacheKeys.plugin.webhookDay`), the same last-24-hours window as before; the same job run twice holds its place; a Redis failure is thrown and the queue tries the job again (a cap open when its store fails is no cap). Tests: `tests/api/plugin-webhooks.spec.ts` (ten deliveries at once against a cap of three pass exactly three; the same job twice counts once), `pinned-request.spec.ts`, the `discardBody` cases of `pinned-https-exchange.spec.ts`, and the unchanged specs of the post and of both deliverers. **Left (rule 12, owner Step 7.3, next PR 7.3-B5b):** (a) the count lives in Redis, so a flush of Redis (or its loss) gives the plugin a new day: accepted, the window is a courtesy limit and the delivery log stays the record; (b) **[closed in 7.3-B5b]** the three debts that were listed with this one and are not a helper: the screens of the plugin that read more than the view shows (a minimal `select`), `detail()` reading the whole catalog for one entry, install against delete at the same instant answering 500 (a row lock), and the team-wide invalidation event for the reads of a plugin (debt (d) of E1, (d) of W1); (c) **[closed in 7.3-B5b]** the data check of manifests already stored against a third language or the limits of a widget (debt (a) of PLG-008): it needs a script over `plugins.manifest` before the registry is opened to third parties; (d) `loopbackExchange` of `local-test-url.ts` (plain http, for a plugin on this machine in a test run) keeps its own request: it is not https and not pinned. (e) the window is scored with the `now()` of the worker that takes the place, so workers whose clocks differ by seconds shift the 24-hour edge by that much: accepted (a cap of a day does not need better), and Redis `TIME` is the way if it ever matters; (f) the cap is taken on EVERY try, not only the first: a retry finds the place its first try took (same delivery id) and goes, and a retry whose first try never took one (Redis down) takes one now or is dropped, so a Redis failure cannot open the cap; the case "a delivery that began is finished" of `plugin-webhooks.spec.ts` now retries the SAME job (it used a new delivery id at attempt 2, which no real queue produces); (h) **Redis down CLOSES the cap** (owner Step 7.3, decided in the review of PR 7.3-B5): `PluginWebhookDayCap.take` throws, the delivery does not start, the queue tries the job again with its own back-off and every try asks for the place again; nothing is sent over the cap and nothing is lost while Redis is back within the retries of the job; a job that runs out of tries is a failed job of the queue (no payload kept: `removeOnFail`), not a failure of the endpoint, so it counts toward turning nothing off; (i) the place and the life of the key are ONE Lua script (`ZADD` and `PEXPIRE` together), so a process that dies cannot leave a key with no end; the window is the last 24 hours (a rolling one, as before: a calendar day would let a burst double at midnight UTC), kept as a sorted set of delivery ids and not an `INCR`, because the same job run twice must hold one place; (j) Redis down also means a job that runs out of tries leaves no log row and no metric: the delivery is lost without the owner seeing it. Owner Step 7.6 (metrics): a counter `webhook_cap_unchecked` on every `take` that throws, with an alert; (k) one installation is held to at most `WebhookLimits.PLUGIN_DAY_CAP_CEILING` (100 000) deliveries a day whatever the manifest says (the manifest keeps its own limit of 1 000 000 and an older manifest is not refused for it): the places live in Redis, one entry per delivery, so the ceiling bounds the memory a hostile or careless plugin can take there (about 10 MB); (l) `assertAnswerReading` refuses at run time an exchange that reads the answer with no ceiling above zero (the union only holds in TypeScript); (g) `PinnedExchangeOptions` is a union: a caller states `maxResponseBytes` or `discardBody: true`, never neither; the test helper `loopbackExchange` of `tests/contracts` and `commandsExchange` honour `discardBody` too.
- [x] **Plugin reads that say less, a lock proved, a read that reaches the team, stored manifests that cannot slip a limit (Step 7.3-B5b, PR `fix/plugin-b5b`; closes (b) and (c) of the 7.3-B5 note, debt (d) of E1 and (d) of W1; rule 12).** (1) **#30, minimal reads.** The catalog of a store reads the columns it draws and `manifest -> 'names'` (a raw statement over `plugins`, run inside the context of the store as the rest of the screen), never the whole manifest; `detail()` reads ONE plugin row (the manifest it draws) and its installation, and `entryOf` (the answer of install, uninstall and the detail) reads the one plugin and counts connections of its own installation only: none of them builds the catalog of the store any more (`entriesOf` is the one builder of an entry). (2) **#30, install against delete.** The lock already stood (N-A7-08, OPS-PLG-308: the install takes the row of the plugin `FOR SHARE`, the deletion takes it `FOR UPDATE`, the revoke and the setup exchange are compare-and-swap on the status); what was missing was the proof that two requests that arrive together end in one of two clear outcomes: `plugin-delete.spec.ts` proves the install side deterministically: a transaction of the test holds the row (an archive in flight) while the install arrives, and the install must wait and then answer 404 with no installation (it dies without the `FOR SHARE`: measured, the plain read ends with an installation on an archived plugin). The deletion side is pinned by outcome only (a held `FOR SHARE` plus an uncommitted installation: 409 `PLUGIN_IN_USE`, nothing deleted); the `FOR UPDATE` of the deletion is defense in depth that no test can see, because the foreign key of the installation maps to the same 409 (measured: the test survives without it). A first version raced two requests and survived both mutants two times of three: dropped. (3) **Team-wide invalidation of a plugin read.** `CONVERSATION_READ` and `CONVERSATION_UNREAD` carry `byPlugin` when the viewer is a plugin (set by `markRead` and `markUnread`); the listener then sends the realtime event to every socket that may see the conversation (`mayAny` over its visibility, the rule of the attention mark) with `userId: null`, so no screen learns which plugin it was; a person's read still reaches only their own tabs. (4) **#33, stored manifests that cannot slip a limit.** `manifestMaxWebhooksPerDay` read an out-of-range or malformed stored cap as NO cap; it now holds it to the nearest edge of the range (a string, a null, NaN or an infinity: the ceiling of the platform, 100 000), and a manifest that names no cap at all is held to the ceiling of the platform too (`PluginWebhookDayCap.take` with `WebhookLimits.PLUGIN_DAY_CAP_CEILING`: the bound that protects Redis (k of 7.3-B5) is no longer skipped by omitting the limit). `PluginApiKeyGuard` holds `plugin_installations.rate_limit_per_minute` (a column with no check) to the range a manifest may ask for (`heldRateLimit`: above the top it is lowered to the top, zero, a negative or no number takes the default of an install), so a row of an older parser or written by hand can neither lift the limit nor shut a plugin out. Already safe and now said: a stored manifest the parser of today refuses is dropped by the widget list, refused at install, and leaves the adapter it had in `remote-channel-sync` (none of them takes a limit away); `pnpm check:plugin-manifests` (`libs/plugins/runtime/tools`) is the data check of PLG-008 (a). Tests: `plugin-manifest.spec.ts` (every shape of the stored cap), `plugin-install-rules.spec.ts` (`heldRateLimit`), `plugin-webhooks.spec.ts` (the ceiling for an undeclared cap and the edges for a stored zero, string and too-large number, through the real deliverer), `realtime.spec.ts` (a plugin read reaches every socket that may see the conversation, with no author, and not another store or a socket that may not see it), `plugin-delete.spec.ts` (the race). **Left (rule 12, owner Step 7.3):** (a) `pnpm check:plugin-manifests` is run by hand over a database: the owner runs it on the development database and before the registry opens to third parties (checklist of Step 7.5); this PR ran it on no real data. (b) A plugin that declared no cap now holds at most 100 000 deliveries a day: a plugin that sent more through a store with many events is dropped (and logged with `attempt: 0`, as any capped delivery) and must declare a cap of its own to be held lower; the figure is the one of 7.3-B5 (k), and raising it is a decision of the owner; a drop caused by the ceiling and one caused by a manifest cap look the same in the log (`attempt: 0`), so Step 7.6 adds a counter (or a reason in the row) that tells them apart. (c) Only the read and unread events of a plugin changed audience; the other events a plugin write publishes were not reviewed here for the same person-only audience: the sweep belongs to the plugin-write steps (E3b, E4a-2) and Step 7.7. (d) a stored daily cap of 0 holds a plugin to 1 delivery a day (strict) while a stored rate limit of 0 takes the default of 60: inconsistent on purpose, both safe (the cap is a courtesy bound, the rate limit must not lock a plugin out); owner Step 7.7. (e) `detail()` reads the installation of the store twice (once for the entry, once for what the screen draws of it), in separate statements, so a revoke landing between them can show an entry and an installation block that disagree for one response; Step 7.7 derives both from one read. A person's read still reaches only their own tabs (pre-existing: the badge of another agent refreshes on its next fetch); whether it too should reach the team is for the inbox steps. (f) The catalog statement is raw SQL, so a column rename of `plugins` is not caught by the compiler: `plugins.spec.ts` and `plugin-delete.spec.ts` read the catalog and fail on it.
